explanation: A starting value taken from the data can never be beaten by the data being unusual, which is why it needs no guarantee. Zero imposes a condition on the input that nothing in the code states or checks.

prompt: An array fault produces a slightly wrong total, and another produces a wildly wrong one. Which is more likely to reach production, and why?
optionA: The wild one, because large numbers are harder to notice
optionB: The slight one, because a plausible total passes the informal checks people actually make
optionC: They are equally likely, since both are faults
optionD: The slight one, because small errors are harder to fix
correctAnswerText: The slight one, because a plausible total passes the informal checks people actually make
explanation: What keeps a fault alive is not its size but whether anybody questions the output. A total that looks about right is accepted; one that is obviously absurd is investigated the first time it appears.

prompt: An approach compares each item with the one after it. It behaves correctly on every array of two or more items that it has been given. Which input breaks it?
optionA: An array of two items, where only one comparison is possible
optionB: An array with repeated values
optionC: An array in reverse order
optionD: An array of exactly one item, where there is no following item to compare with
correctAnswerText: An array of exactly one item, where there is no following item to compare with
explanation: Reading ahead by one needs a successor to exist, and only a single item leaves none. Two items give exactly one comparison, which is the smallest case that works rather than the smallest that fails.

prompt: An approach compares each item with the one after it. What does it produce for an empty array?
optionA: Nothing, and correctly so; there are no pairs and the loop runs zero times
optionB: A failure, because there is no first item to read
optionC: A single comparison against nothing
optionD: The same result as for a single item
correctAnswerText: Nothing, and correctly so; there are no pairs and the loop runs zero times
explanation: With no items there is nothing to start from either, so the loop never begins and no access is attempted. Empty and single-item input fail in different ways here, which is why both are worth trying.

prompt: A search reports the position of a value. What should it report when the value is absent, and why not simply zero?
optionA: Zero, which is the natural empty answer
optionB: The length of the array, which is always safe
optionC: Something no valid position can be, since zero is itself a valid position and would be indistinguishable from a match at the front
optionD: Nothing; it should stop with an error instead
correctAnswerText: Something no valid position can be, since zero is itself a valid position and would be indistinguishable from a match at the front
explanation: Counting from zero means the first position and the "not found" answer would collide, so the value has to lie outside the range of positions. Being absent is an expected outcome rather than a fault, so stopping is too strong.

prompt: A reversal using two positions moving toward each other is run on an array of exactly one item. What happens?
optionA: The item is swapped with itself and lost
optionB: Nothing; the two positions already meet, so no swap is performed and the array is correct
optionC: The method fails, because there is no pair to swap
optionD: The positions cross immediately and the loop runs endlessly
correctAnswerText: Nothing; the two positions already meet, so no swap is performed and the array is correct
explanation: The stopping condition is already satisfied before any swap, so the loop does no work — and doing no work is exactly right for reversing one item. An edge case that needs no special handling is worth recognising as such.

prompt: An approach is correct for arrays of two or more items and wrong for one item. Two fixes are proposed: add a special case for a single item, or change the loop bound so the single-item case falls out correctly. Which is preferable?
optionA: The special case, because it leaves the working behaviour untouched
optionB: Either; both produce the right answer
optionC: The special case, because loop bounds are harder to reason about
optionD: Changing the bound where it works, since a special case is another path that must stay correct as the code changes
correctAnswerText: Changing the bound where it works, since a special case is another path that must stay correct as the code changes
explanation: Both fix the symptom and they leave different things behind. A bound that handles every size needs no upkeep; a special case has to be remembered by everyone who edits the code afterwards.

prompt: A collection is searched thousands of times a day and added to twice a day. Both keeping it sorted and leaving it unsorted would work. Which arrangement suits it?
optionA: Keep it sorted, since the cost falls on the rare operation and the frequent one becomes much cheaper
optionB: Leave it unsorted, since sorting costs more than searching
optionC: Leave it unsorted, since insertions must stay fast
optionD: Either; the usage pattern does not affect the choice
correctAnswerText: Keep it sorted, since the cost falls on the rare operation and the frequent one becomes much cheaper
explanation: The usage decides it: sorting is paid twice a day and repaid thousands of times. The same two arrangements would be ranked the other way round if the frequencies were reversed.

prompt: A collection is added to constantly and searched once a week. Which arrangement suits it, and what does the choice cost?
optionA: Keep it sorted, so the weekly search is fast
optionB: Keep it sorted, since sorted data is always preferable
optionC: Leave it unsorted; the weekly search costs a full traversal, which is far less than keeping every insertion in order
optionD: Either; a weekly search is too rare to matter
correctAnswerText: Leave it unsorted; the weekly search costs a full traversal, which is far less than keeping every insertion in order
explanation: Reversing the frequencies reverses the answer, which is the point: the cost of order is paid on every insertion, and here insertions are what dominate. The weekly traversal is a real cost and a small one.

prompt: A collection is both added to and searched constantly, in roughly equal measure. What follows about the choice between sorted and unsorted?
optionA: Sorted, since searching is the more important operation
optionB: Neither arrangement is clearly better, and the answer depends on measuring the two costs rather than reasoning about them
optionC: Unsorted, since insertion is the more frequent operation
optionD: Sorted, since a tie should be broken in favour of order
correctAnswerText: Neither arrangement is clearly better, and the answer depends on measuring the two costs rather than reasoning about them
explanation: The rule that decides the two lopsided cases gives no answer when neither dominates, and inventing a tiebreak dresses a guess as a principle. Recognising where a rule stops applying is part of using it.

prompt: A team keeps a collection sorted so that searches are fast, and later discovers that almost all the searches are for the most recently added item. What does that change?
optionA: Nothing; sorted data is faster to search whatever is being sought
optionB: The ordering becomes more valuable, since recent items are at one end
optionC: The collection should be sorted in the opposite direction
optionD: The ordering buys much less than expected, since the newest item could be found immediately without it
correctAnswerText: The ordering buys much less than expected, since the newest item could be found immediately without it
explanation: A cost decision rests on what the operations actually are, and "search" turned out to mean something narrower than assumed. Sorting by value does not put the newest item anywhere in particular, so reversing the order does not help either.

prompt: The text is "my code". What character is at position 0?
optionA: y
optionB: m
optionC: c
optionD: There is no position 0
correctAnswerText: m
explanation: Positions are counted from zero, so the first character sits at position 0. Counting from one would give the second character instead.

prompt: The text is "my code". What character is at position 2?
optionA: c
optionB: y
optionC: o
optionD: A space
correctAnswerText: A space
explanation: A space is a character like any other and occupies its own position, so it sits between the two words at position 2. Skipping it shifts every later position by one.

prompt: The text is "my code". At what position is the letter c?
explanation: Counting m as 0, y as 1 and the space as 2 puts c at position 3. Answering 2 is what ignoring the space produces.

prompt: The text is "go now". What is at the last valid position?
optionA: o
optionB: A space
optionC: w
optionD: There is none until the text is complete
correctAnswerText: w
explanation: The last valid position holds the final character, which is w. Answering o stops one short, which is what treating the length as the last position and then correcting twice produces.

prompt: The text is "a b c", with single spaces between the letters. How many positions does it occupy, and what is at position 1?
optionA: Three positions, and position 1 holds b
optionB: Five positions, and position 1 holds a space
optionC: Five positions, and position 1 holds b
optionD: Three positions, and position 1 holds a space
correctAnswerText: Five positions, and position 1 holds a space
explanation: Three letters and two spaces occupy five positions in all, and the first space follows the first letter. Counting only the letters gives three and moves every later character.

prompt: What is the length of the text "data set"?
explanation: Seven letters and one space make a length of 8. Answering 7 omits the space, and 2 counts the words rather than the characters.

prompt: What is the length of the text "hi " — the two letters followed by a single trailing space?
explanation: A trailing space is a character and is counted, so the length is three. It is invisible when the text is displayed, which is exactly why it is missed.

prompt: What is the length of text containing no characters at all?
optionB: Undefined
optionD: It cannot exist
explanation: Empty text is ordinary text whose length is zero, and it has no valid positions. That is different from text containing a single space, whose length is one.

prompt: A program holds the text "career" and reports its length. What is reported?
optionD: career
explanation: Six characters give a length of 6. Answering 5 or 7 is off by one at an end, and reporting the text itself answers a different question.

prompt: Do the two pieces of text "Yes" and "yes" compare as equal?
optionA: Yes; they spell the same word
optionB: Yes; comparison ignores case
optionC: It cannot be decided without knowing the language
optionD: No; the first characters differ
correctAnswerText: No; the first characters differ
explanation: A comparison examines the characters, and an upper-case letter is a different character from its lower-case form. Spelling the same word is not the same as being the same text.

prompt: Do the two pieces of text "OK" and "OK" compare as equal?
optionA: Yes; every character matches
optionB: No; identical text never compares equal
optionC: Yes, but only if the two are stored in the same place
optionD: It depends on how the text was created
correctAnswerText: Yes; every character matches
explanation: Comparison is about the characters and nothing else, so identical characters compare equal however each piece of text came to exist.

prompt: Do the two pieces of text " ok" and "ok" compare as equal — the first with a single leading space?
optionA: Yes; a leading space is ignored
optionB: Yes; both contain the same letters
optionC: No; the first has an extra character at the front
optionD: No; the two have the same length but differ in case
correctAnswerText: No; the first has an extra character at the front
explanation: A leading space is a character, so the two pieces differ in both length and content. Nothing strips spaces on the way into a comparison.

prompt: A program compares a typed answer with the stored answer "Blue" and rejects "blue" as wrong. What change would accept both?
optionA: Compare the lengths instead of the characters
optionB: Convert both to the same case before comparing
optionC: Store the answer in lower case only
optionD: Nothing; the two are genuinely different answers
correctAnswerText: Convert both to the same case before comparing
explanation: Bringing both sides to a common case removes the distinction before the comparison sees it. Storing the answer in lower case alone would still reject a capitalised entry.

prompt: The text is "abcdef". A range starts at position 1 and stops before position 4. What does it produce?
optionA: bcde
optionB: abcd
optionC: bc
optionD: bcd
correctAnswerText: bcd
explanation: Positions 1, 2 and 3 are taken and position 4 is not, because the range stops before it. Including the end gives one character too many.

prompt: The text is "network". A range starts at position 3 and stops before position 3. What does it produce?
optionA: Nothing; the range is empty
optionB: w
optionC: wo
optionD: The whole text
correctAnswerText: Nothing; the range is empty
explanation: A range that starts where it stops contains no positions at all, so the result is empty. That is a legitimate outcome rather than an error, and it is what an off-by-one in the wrong direction quietly produces.

prompt: A variable holds "Report". An operation converting it to upper case is performed, and its result is not stored anywhere. What does the variable hold afterwards?
optionA: REPORT
optionB: report
optionC: Report
optionD: Nothing; the value was consumed
correctAnswerText: Report
explanation: The operation builds new text and hands it back, leaving the original untouched. Discarding the result therefore changes nothing at all.

prompt: A variable holds " total " with a space at each end. A trimming operation is applied and its result is assigned to a second variable. What do the two variables hold?
optionA: Both hold "total"
optionB: The first still holds " total " and the second holds "total"
optionC: The first holds "total" and the second holds " total "
optionD: Both hold " total "
correctAnswerText: The first still holds " total " and the second holds "total"
explanation: Trimming produces new text and the original is unchanged, so the two variables differ. Assigning the result is what makes the trimmed version available at all.

prompt: The text is "banana". A search for "an" reports the position of the first match. What does it report?
explanation: The first "an" begins at position 1, counting b as 0. Position 3 is where the second match begins, which is what reporting the last match would give.

prompt: The text is "banana". A search for "xy" is performed. What should the result be?
optionA: A value that is not a valid position, marking absence
optionB: 0, since nothing was found
optionC: The length of the text
optionD: An error, since the search failed
correctAnswerText: A value that is not a valid position, marking absence
explanation: Zero is a perfectly valid position and would be indistinguishable from a match at the front, so absence has to be reported by something outside the range of positions. Not finding something is an ordinary outcome rather than a failure.

prompt: A program treats a search result of 0 as meaning "not found" and reports that a value is missing when it is actually the first thing in the text. The search itself returns the correct position. What is wrong?
optionA: The search is returning the wrong position
optionB: The value being searched for is empty
optionC: Zero is a real position, so it cannot also stand for absence
optionD: The text has a leading space, shifting the position
correctAnswerText: Zero is a real position, so it cannot also stand for absence
explanation: The search is stated to be correct, so the fault is in how its answer is read. A match at the very front is the one case where a valid position collides with the marker chosen for absence.

prompt: The text "red,green,blue" is split on the comma. How many pieces result?
explanation: Two separators divide the text into three pieces. The count of pieces is always one more than the count of separators when none of them sit at an end.

prompt: A line ends with the separator it uses: "north;south;" split on the semicolon. What is the final piece?
optionA: south, because a trailing separator is ignored
optionB: A semicolon, because the separator is kept
optionC: There is no final piece; the split yields two
optionD: An empty piece, following the last semicolon
correctAnswerText: An empty piece, following the last semicolon
explanation: A separator at the end still separates, so something follows it and that something is empty. The separator itself never appears inside any piece.

prompt: The text "a,,b" is split on the comma and a program reports two pieces. It expects one piece per value and the two commas are genuinely present in the data. What has it done wrong?
optionA: It has discarded the empty piece between the two commas, which the split produces
optionB: It has treated the two commas as one separator, which is correct
optionC: It has included the comma in one of the pieces
optionD: It has split on the wrong character
correctAnswerText: It has discarded the empty piece between the two commas, which the split produces
explanation: Consecutive separators produce an empty piece between them, so the split gives three. A program reporting two has dropped it, which loses the information that a value was missing there.

prompt: The pieces red, green and blue are joined with a comma between them. What is produced?
optionA: red,green,blue,
optionB: ,red,green,blue
optionC: red,green,blue
optionD: redgreenblue
correctAnswerText: red,green,blue
explanation: Separators go between pieces, so three pieces need two separators and none at either end. A trailing separator is what building the text piece by piece without care produces.

prompt: Five pieces are joined with a separator between them. How many separators appear?
explanation: Separators sit in the gaps between pieces, and five pieces have 4 gaps. Answering 5 places one after the last piece as well.

prompt: A program builds a list by adding each value followed by a comma, and the result always ends with a stray comma. Every value is present and in the right order. What is the smallest change that fixes it?
optionA: Remove the last value as well as the comma
optionB: Add the values in reverse order
optionC: Use a different separator character
optionD: Put the separator before each value except the first, rather than after each value
correctAnswerText: Put the separator before each value except the first, rather than after each value
explanation: Every value being correct places the fault in where the separator goes rather than in the data. Moving it to precede each value except the first gives exactly one separator per gap and none at either end.

prompt: Two entries display as "cat" and "cat", and a comparison reports them as different. The second has a trailing space. Why do they not match?
optionA: The second contains one more character than the first
optionB: The two differ in case
optionC: The two have the same length and differ in content
optionD: A comparison cannot be relied on for text
correctAnswerText: The second contains one more character than the first
explanation: A trailing space is a character that shows as nothing, so the two pieces differ in length while looking identical. Nothing about the comparison is unreliable.

prompt: Two entries both display as "no data" and both are seven characters long, yet they do not match. One uses a single space and the other uses a different invisible character of the same width. What is the cause?
optionA: One of them has a trailing space
optionB: The two differ in case somewhere
optionC: The invisible characters differ, so the two are different text of the same length
optionD: Equal-length text always matches, so the report is wrong
correctAnswerText: The invisible characters differ, so the two are different text of the same length
explanation: Equal length rules out a missing or extra character, and identical appearance rules out a visible difference — which leaves a character that is invisible and not the one expected. Length is a weaker check than it looks.

prompt: A lookup fails for entries typed by hand and succeeds for the same entries loaded from a file. The values look identical in both cases and the lookup itself is correct. What is the likely cause?
optionA: The typed entries differ in case
optionB: The typed entries carry leading or trailing spaces that the file entries do not
optionC: The lookup is case-sensitive and the file is not
optionD: The file entries were converted to a different format
correctAnswerText: The typed entries carry leading or trailing spaces that the file entries do not
explanation: Identical appearance with different behaviour, split cleanly by how the value arrived, points at something invisible that typing adds. Case would be visible in the comparison, and the lookup is stated to be correct.

prompt: A traversal counts the vowels in "open air". How many does it find?
explanation: The vowels are o, e, a and i, giving a count of 4. The space is not a vowel and the consonants are not counted, so 8 reports the length instead.

prompt: A traversal counts characters in "go on" that are not spaces. How many does it find?
explanation: Five positions hold four letters and one space, so the count excluding spaces is 4. Answering 5 counts everything, which is the length rather than the count asked for.

prompt: A traversal building a reversed copy of "abc" produces "cba" correctly, and on "ab c" it produces "c ba". The traversal visits every position exactly once. Is that correct?
optionA: No; the space should have stayed where it was
optionB: No; the space should have been removed
optionC: Yes; reversing includes the space, and "c ba" is the reverse of "ab c"
optionD: No; the words should have been reversed rather than the characters
correctAnswerText: Yes; reversing includes the space, and "c ba" is the reverse of "ab c"
explanation: Reversing the characters moves every one of them, the space included, and the result is exactly what that gives. Expecting the space to stay put confuses reversing the characters with reversing the words.

prompt: A check compares the first character with the last, the second with the second-last, and so on, treating case as significant and spaces as characters. Does "Level" pass?
optionA: Yes; the letters read the same in both directions
optionB: No; the first character is upper case and the last is lower case
optionC: No; the text has an odd number of characters
optionD: Yes; case is ignored in a symmetry check
correctAnswerText: No; the first character is upper case and the last is lower case
explanation: The stem states that case is significant, and L does not match l. Reading the word as symmetric requires ignoring exactly the thing the check is told to respect.

prompt: The same check is applied to "abcba", comparing from both ends inward. It reports success after 2 comparisons. Someone expects 5. Why is 2 correct?
optionA: The check stops as soon as it finds one match
optionB: The check compares only the outermost pair
optionC: The count should be 5; the report is wrong
optionD: Each comparison settles two characters, and the middle character needs none
correctAnswerText: Each comparison settles two characters, and the middle character needs none
explanation: Five characters form two pairs with one left in the middle, and a character compared with itself proves nothing. Expecting one comparison per character double-counts every pair.

prompt: Text is built by repeatedly adding one character to the end of existing text, producing new text each time. What happens to the work as the text grows?
optionA: It rises, because each addition copies everything built so far
optionB: It stays the same, since one character is added each time
optionC: It falls, since the text is already partly built
optionD: It stays the same, since the code is one line either way
correctAnswerText: It rises, because each addition copies everything built so far
explanation: Each addition produces new text containing everything that came before, so the copying grows with the length. That both approaches are one line of code is exactly why the difference is invisible in the source.

prompt: Two methods build the same text and produce identical results. One adds to existing text repeatedly and the other collects the pieces and joins them once at the end. Which does more work, and why?
optionA: The join, because it must examine every piece at the end
optionB: Neither; identical results mean identical work
optionC: The repeated addition, because every step copies what has already been built
optionD: The repeated addition, because it uses more lines of code
correctAnswerText: The repeated addition, because every step copies what has already been built
explanation: Identical results settle correctness and say nothing about cost. Collecting and joining once copies each piece a single time, while repeated addition copies the growing result again at every step.

prompt: A traversal over text produces output missing its final character. What is the fault?
optionA: The loop starts one position too late
optionB: The loop stops one position before the end
optionC: The output is being built in reverse
optionD: The final character is a space and was skipped
correctAnswerText: The loop stops one position before the end
explanation: Which end the missing character came from identifies which bound is wrong. Starting late would drop the first character instead.

prompt: A program builds a comma-separated list and the output ends with a comma but is otherwise correct. Every value appears exactly once and in order. What is the fault?
optionA: A separator is added before every value, including the first
optionB: The final value is missing and only its separator remains
optionC: The values are being joined in the wrong order
optionD: A separator is added after every value, including the last
correctAnswerText: A separator is added after every value, including the last
explanation: A trailing separator with every value present places the fault at the end rather than in the data. Adding the separator before each value would have produced a leading one instead, which is a distinguishable symptom.

prompt: Two faults produce similar-looking output: one drops the last character of the text, and one adds a trailing separator. How can they be told apart from the output alone?
optionA: One output is shorter than it should be and the other longer, and only the second ends in a separator
optionB: They cannot be told apart from the output alone
optionC: Only the first changes the length of the output
optionD: Only the second affects the order of the values
correctAnswerText: One output is shorter than it should be and the other longer, and only the second ends in a separator
explanation: Each fault leaves its own signature: a missing character shortens the result, and a stray separator lengthens it and is visible at the end. Reading the output carefully is what separates two faults that both look like an off-by-one.

prompt: A program strips spaces from the ends of every entry and a lookup still fails for one of them. What is the next thing to check, and why?
optionA: Whether the lookup is case-sensitive, since stripping does not affect case
optionB: Whether the entry is longer than the others, since length affects matching
optionC: Whether the entry contains an invisible character that is not a space, since stripping removes only what it recognises
optionD: Whether stripping was applied to both sides of the comparison
correctAnswerText: Whether the entry contains an invisible character that is not a space, since stripping removes only what it recognises
explanation: Stripping handles the spaces it knows about and leaves anything else, so an entry that still fails after stripping points at a character that looks like a space and is not. Case is worth checking too and would not have been masked by the stripping.

prompt: A text fault produces output that is obviously mangled, and another produces output that looks right and is subtly wrong. Which costs more, and why?
optionA: The mangled one, because more of the output is affected
optionB: The subtle one, because mangled output is noticed immediately while plausible output is used
optionC: They cost the same, since both are faults
optionD: The subtle one, because it is harder to reproduce
correctAnswerText: The subtle one, because mangled output is noticed immediately while plausible output is used
explanation: What limits the damage a fault does is whether anyone notices it. Obviously broken output is investigated the first time it appears; output that reads correctly travels onward and is acted on.

prompt: A symmetry check comparing from both ends inward is given empty text. It reports success without making any comparison. Is that correct?
optionA: No; it should have failed, since there is nothing to check
optionB: No; it should have stopped with an error
optionC: Yes, but only because the check does not handle empty text
optionD: Yes; empty text is trivially symmetric and there is nothing to compare
correctAnswerText: Yes; empty text is trivially symmetric and there is nothing to compare
explanation: The check reports failure only when a pair disagrees, and with no pairs there is no disagreement. Reporting success is the right answer rather than an accident of how the loop is written.

prompt: A traversal counting vowels is given empty text. What does it produce?
optionA: 0, which is correct and needs no special case
optionB: A failure, because there is nothing to examine
optionC: Nothing at all, because the loop never runs
optionD: An error, because the counter was never used
correctAnswerText: 0, which is correct and needs no special case
explanation: The loop runs zero times and the counter keeps the zero it started at, which is the right answer for counting nothing. The initialisation is what makes the empty case safe.

prompt: An approach reads the first character of text in order to decide something. What does it do on empty text?
optionA: It reads an empty character and continues
optionB: It returns without doing anything
optionC: It fails, because there is no first character to read
optionD: It reads a space, which stands in for the missing character
correctAnswerText: It fails, because there is no first character to read
explanation: Reading position 0 requires a character to be there, and empty text has none. Nothing substitutes a blank on the program's behalf, which is why this case has to be handled deliberately.

prompt: Splitting empty text on a comma produces how many pieces?
optionA: None
optionB: One, which is itself empty
optionC: Two, both empty
optionD: It fails, since there is nothing to split
correctAnswerText: One, which is itself empty
explanation: A split always produces one more piece than the separators it finds, and finding none gives one piece — the whole of the input, which happens to be empty. Answering none confuses an empty piece with no piece.

prompt: An approach works for text of two characters or more and fails for one character. Two fixes are proposed: a special case for single-character text, or a change to the loop bound. Which is preferable?
optionA: The special case, because it leaves working behaviour untouched
optionB: Either; both give the right answer
optionC: The special case, because bounds are harder to reason about
optionD: The bound, where it can be made to cover the case, since a special case is another path to keep correct
correctAnswerText: The bound, where it can be made to cover the case, since a special case is another path to keep correct
explanation: Both remove the symptom and they leave different things behind. A bound that handles every length needs no upkeep; a special case has to be remembered by everyone who edits the code afterwards.

prompt: Values must be extracted from lines where fields are separated by commas, and some fields are empty so consecutive commas occur. Which approach handles it?
optionA: Split on the comma and keep every piece, empty ones included
optionB: Split on the comma and discard empty pieces
optionC: Split on runs of commas, treating consecutive ones as one separator
optionD: Search for each field by position within the line
correctAnswerText: Split on the comma and keep every piece, empty ones included
explanation: Empty fields have to survive, or later fields shift into the wrong positions. Both of the discarding approaches work on tidy data and silently corrupt exactly the lines the stem describes.

prompt: Words must be counted in a line where words may be separated by more than one space. Which approach handles it?
optionA: Split on a single space and count the pieces
optionB: Count the spaces and add one
optionC: Split on runs of spaces, so that consecutive spaces produce no empty words
optionD: Count the characters and divide by the average word length
correctAnswerText: Split on runs of spaces, so that consecutive spaces produce no empty words
explanation: Runs of spaces have to collapse here, which is the opposite of what the comma case needed — the awkward input decides which behaviour is wanted. Splitting on a single space would count an empty piece for each extra space.

prompt: Two text tasks look alike: one must preserve empty pieces between separators, and one must ignore them. What does that show about choosing an approach?
optionA: One of the two tasks must have been described wrongly
optionB: The right behaviour is decided by the task rather than by the operation, so the same split can be right in one and wrong in the other
optionC: The same approach should be used for both, for consistency
optionD: Empty pieces should always be discarded, since they carry no data
correctAnswerText: The right behaviour is decided by the task rather than by the operation, so the same split can be right in one and wrong in the other
explanation: An empty field between two commas carries real information — that a value was missing — while an extra space between words carries none. The operation is identical and the requirement is not.

prompt: A text task can be done with one traversal that does everything, or with three simple traversals in sequence. Both are correct. On what grounds should the choice be made?
optionA: On the single traversal, since fewer passes is always better
optionB: On the three traversals, since simpler code is always better
optionC: On neither; correct approaches are interchangeable
optionD: On whether reading the data three times costs enough to matter, weighed against three simpler pieces of code
correctAnswerText: On whether reading the data three times costs enough to matter, weighed against three simpler pieces of code
explanation: Correctness no longer separates them, so the remaining differences are cost and clarity, and which dominates depends on the size of the data. Neither "fewer passes" nor "simpler code" is a rule that holds without knowing that.

prompt: In a web exchange, which side sends first?
optionA: The server, with a response
optionB: The client, with a request
optionC: Either; whichever is ready first
optionD: Both at once, and the exchange settles afterwards
correctAnswerText: The client, with a request
explanation: An exchange begins with a request and the response answers it. A server that could start the conversation would have to know which client to speak to and when.

prompt: How many responses does a server send for one request?
optionA: None; the response is optional
optionB: As many as it needs, over time
optionC: Two: one to acknowledge and one with the answer
optionD: One
correctAnswerText: One
explanation: One request is answered by one response, even when that response reports a failure. A client waiting for an answer that never comes has no way to tell success from silence.

prompt: A page is loaded and then the reader does nothing for an hour. What is passing between the browser and the server during that hour?
optionA: Nothing, unless something on the page asks for more
optionB: A continuous stream keeping the page alive
optionC: A response every few seconds, confirming the page is still valid
optionD: The page itself, sent repeatedly
correctAnswerText: Nothing, unless something on the page asks for more
explanation: The exchange finished when the response arrived, and nothing continues by itself. Anything further requires a new request.

prompt: A browser asks for a page and the server has no such page. What does the server send?
optionA: Nothing, since there is nothing to send
optionB: The nearest page it does have
optionC: A response saying the page was not found
optionD: A request asking the browser to try again
correctAnswerText: A response saying the page was not found
explanation: Every request gets a response, and reporting an absence is one of the things a response is for. Sending nothing would leave the browser unable to distinguish a missing page from a broken connection.

prompt: A page contains three images. How many exchanges take place to display it fully?
optionA: One; the page arrives complete
optionB: Four: one for the page and one for each image
optionC: Two: one for the page and one for the images together
optionD: Three: one per image, with the page included in the first
correctAnswerText: Four: one for the page and one for each image
explanation: The page arrives first and names the images, and each of those is fetched by its own request. The browser cannot ask for the images before it has read the page that mentions them.

prompt: A request uses the method that means "give me this". What is it asking for?
optionA: A change to be made on the server
optionB: A record to be deleted
optionC: A new record to be created
optionD: Data, without changing anything
correctAnswerText: Data, without changing anything
explanation: A fetch states an intention to read. The other three describe changes, which a different method exists to express.

prompt: A request uses the method that means "here is something to store". What is it asking for?
optionA: A change on the server
optionB: Data to be returned unchanged
optionC: The connection to be closed
optionD: The page to be reloaded
correctAnswerText: A change on the server
explanation: A submitting method states an intention to change something. The response may still return data, and that is not what the method is for.

prompt: Who decides which method a request uses?
optionA: The server, when it decides how to answer
optionB: The protocol, according to the address
optionC: The client, when it makes the request
optionD: The browser, according to the page size
correctAnswerText: The client, when it makes the request
explanation: The method states what the client intends, so the client chooses it. The server may refuse, which is a different matter from choosing.

prompt: A request made with a fetch method changes a record on the server. Is that possible, and is it appropriate?
optionA: Impossible; the protocol prevents it
optionB: Possible, because nothing enforces the meaning, and inappropriate, because everything treats a fetch as safe to repeat
optionC: Possible and appropriate, if it is what the application needs
optionD: Impossible; the server would refuse the request
correctAnswerText: Possible, because nothing enforces the meaning, and inappropriate, because everything treats a fetch as safe to repeat
explanation: The method is a statement of intent rather than a rule the protocol enforces, so a fetch that changes things will work. Everything from browsers to caches assumes a fetch is repeatable, which is what makes it a poor choice rather than an impossible one.

prompt: A response carries a status in the 400 range. What does that indicate?
optionA: The server failed while handling the request
optionB: The request succeeded
optionC: The request should be sent to a different address
optionD: The request was refused because of something about the request itself
correctAnswerText: The request was refused because of something about the request itself
explanation: The 400 range places the problem on the client side — a bad address, missing identification, a malformed body. A server failure falls in a different range.

prompt: A response carries a status in the 500 range. What does that indicate?
optionA: The server failed while handling a request that may have been perfectly valid
optionB: The request was malformed
optionC: The request succeeded
optionD: The address does not exist
correctAnswerText: The server failed while handling a request that may have been perfectly valid
explanation: The 500 range says the fault is on the server side, so resending the same request unchanged is reasonable. A malformed request would be reported in the 400 range instead.

prompt: A response carries a status in the 300 range, telling the client to look elsewhere. Did the request fail?
optionA: Yes; anything other than success is a failure
optionB: Yes; the resource does not exist
optionC: No; the client is being told where to go next, which is a normal outcome
optionD: No; the response is the resource itself
correctAnswerText: No; the client is being told where to go next, which is a normal outcome
explanation: A redirection is an instruction rather than a failure, and following it usually succeeds. Treating every non-success status as a failure loses that distinction.

prompt: A request returns a success status and an empty body. Did it fail?
optionA: Yes; an empty body means the server failed
optionB: No; the request succeeded and the answer happens to be empty
optionC: Yes; a success status with no data is a contradiction
optionD: It cannot be said without the status number
correctAnswerText: No; the request succeeded and the answer happens to be empty
explanation: A search that matched nothing succeeds and returns nothing, which is exactly this. Reading an empty answer as a failure confuses "no results" with "no answer".

prompt: A request shows: a method, an address, several lines of the form name: value, a blank line, and then some data. Which part are the name-and-value lines?
optionA: The body, which carries the data
optionB: The address, split across lines
optionC: The status, reporting the outcome
optionD: The headers, which describe the message
correctAnswerText: The headers, which describe the message
explanation: Headers sit between the first line and the blank line and describe the message rather than carrying its content. The data after the blank line is the body.

prompt: In the same request, what separates the headers from the body?
optionA: A blank line
optionB: A header naming the body's length
optionC: The address, which comes between them
optionD: Nothing; the reader has to infer where the body begins
correctAnswerText: A blank line
explanation: A blank line marks the end of the headers, which is what lets a reader know where the body starts without counting. A length header describes the body and does not delimit it.

prompt: A client makes a request, and then a second one a minute later. What does the server remember about the first by default?
optionA: Everything, for as long as the browser stays open
optionB: The address requested, but not the data sent
optionC: Nothing; each request arrives without any memory of the last
optionD: Whether the client was logged in
correctAnswerText: Nothing; each request arrives without any memory of the last
explanation: Each request is independent, and anything the server is to know must arrive with it. That is why identifying information travels in every request rather than being established once.

prompt: How does a server recognise the same user across several requests, given that it remembers nothing by default?
optionA: The connection stays open and identifies the user
optionB: Something identifying is sent with each request, and the server looks it up
optionC: The server recognises the address the requests come from
optionD: The browser tells the server it is the same user, and the server trusts it
correctAnswerText: Something identifying is sent with each request, and the server looks it up
explanation: Recognition is rebuilt on every request from something the client sends. An address identifies a network location rather than a person, and many people can share one.

prompt: A page must show a list of orders without changing anything. Which method fits?
optionA: A submitting method, because data is being returned
optionB: A deleting method, because the list may shrink
optionC: Either; the method makes no difference for reading
optionD: A fetch, because nothing is being changed
correctAnswerText: A fetch, because nothing is being changed
explanation: The method states intent, and the intent here is to read. Everything that handles the request is entitled to assume a fetch is safe to repeat.

prompt: A form places an order. What goes wrong if it is submitted with a fetch?
optionA: Reloading the page or following a link back can place the order again
optionB: The order will not be recorded at all
optionC: The server will refuse the request
optionD: Nothing; the method is a matter of style
correctAnswerText: Reloading the page or following a link back can place the order again
explanation: A fetch is treated as repeatable by browsers, caches and users, so a request that changes something can be replayed. The order is recorded perfectly well the first time, which is what makes the problem easy to miss.

prompt: A team reports that their "delete" links occasionally remove records nobody asked to remove. The links use a fetch method and are working exactly as written. What is happening?
optionA: The server is deleting records at random
optionB: The links are pointing at the wrong records
optionC: Something that follows links automatically is visiting them, and a fetch is assumed safe to follow
optionD: The requests are being sent twice by the browser
correctAnswerText: Something that follows links automatically is visiting them, and a fetch is assumed safe to follow
explanation: Anything that prefetches or crawls links treats a fetch as harmless, so a fetch that deletes gets triggered by something that never intended to. The links work as written, which is exactly the problem.

prompt: A request returns a status in the 400 range. Where should the investigation start?
optionA: With the server logs, since the server sent the status
optionB: With the request: its address, its headers and its body
optionC: With the network, since the request travelled
optionD: With the browser version
correctAnswerText: With the request: its address, its headers and its body
explanation: The status names the side at fault, and the 400 range points at the request. Server logs are worth reading and start further from the evidence.

prompt: A request returns a status in the 500 range and the same request succeeded an hour ago, unchanged. Where is the fault?
optionA: In the request, which must have changed
optionB: In the address, which must be wrong
optionC: In the network, which must have dropped the request
optionD: On the server; the request is the same one that worked
correctAnswerText: On the server; the request is the same one that worked
explanation: An unchanged request that used to work rules out the request itself, and the status already places the fault on the server side. A dropped request would produce no status at all.

prompt: A page shows no data. The request returned a success status with an empty body, and the server logs record no errors. What is the most likely explanation?
optionA: The request succeeded and matched nothing, so the fault is in what was asked for rather than in the exchange
optionB: The server failed silently
optionC: The address is wrong, so nothing was found
optionD: The response was lost in transit
correctAnswerText: The request succeeded and matched nothing, so the fault is in what was asked for rather than in the exchange
explanation: A success status with clean logs means the exchange worked, so an empty page is an answer rather than a failure. A wrong address would have produced a status in the 400 range.

prompt: An address must identify one particular order. Where does the identifier belong?
optionA: In the query, because it is a value
optionB: In a header, because it is metadata
optionC: In the path, because it names which resource is wanted
optionD: In the body, because a fetch may carry one
correctAnswerText: In the path, because it names which resource is wanted
explanation: The path names what is being asked for, so an identifier that selects a single thing belongs there. The query narrows or modifies a collection rather than naming a member of it.

prompt: An address must request all orders placed in March. Where does the month belong?
optionA: In the path, because it identifies which orders
optionB: In the query, because it filters a collection rather than naming one order
optionC: In a header, because it is a condition
optionD: Either; the two are interchangeable
correctAnswerText: In the query, because it filters a collection rather than naming one order
explanation: The resource being asked for is the collection of orders, and March narrows it. Putting a filter in the path implies a different resource for every possible filter.

prompt: A team's addresses put filters in the path, so every filter combination is a different address. Every address they have built works correctly. What does the design cost them?
optionA: Nothing; the addresses work
optionB: The server cannot tell one filter from another
optionC: The addresses become too long to send
optionD: A new address has to be defined for each combination, and nothing can be filtered in a way nobody anticipated
correctAnswerText: A new address has to be defined for each combination, and nothing can be filtered in a way nobody anticipated
explanation: The design works, which is why it survives. What it gives up is the ability to combine filters freely, since each combination is a separate address somebody has to add.

prompt: A request carries a header stating that the body is in a particular format. What does that tell the server?
optionA: How to interpret the body it has been sent
optionB: That the body has been converted into that format
optionC: That the server must reply in that format
optionD: That the body is valid
correctAnswerText: How to interpret the body it has been sent
explanation: The header describes the message so the other side knows how to read it. Nothing converts or validates the body because a header says so.

prompt: A request carries a header stating a format that does not match the body actually sent. What happens?
optionA: The server detects the real format and uses it
optionB: The protocol rejects the request before it arrives
optionC: The server tries to read the body as the stated format and fails or misreads it
optionD: The header is ignored, since the body speaks for itself
correctAnswerText: The server tries to read the body as the stated format and fails or misreads it
explanation: A header is a claim, and the receiver acts on it. Nothing checks the claim against the body, which is why a wrong header produces a confusing failure rather than a clear one.

prompt: A server rejects a request as malformed. The body is exactly what the server expects, and the address and method are correct. What should be checked next?
optionA: The server's available memory
optionB: The header describing the body's format, which may not match what was sent
optionC: Whether the body is too long
optionD: Whether the request was sent twice
correctAnswerText: The header describing the body's format, which may not match what was sent
explanation: A correct body rejected as malformed points at how the body was described rather than at its content. The header and the body are two separate claims and only one of them has been verified.

prompt: A secure connection is in use. What does that mainly indicate?
optionA: That the site is trustworthy
optionB: That the site has no server
optionC: That the browser is working offline
optionD: That the exchange is encrypted while it travels
correctAnswerText: That the exchange is encrypted while it travels
explanation: Encryption protects the data in transit and says nothing about who is at the other end or what they do with it. A dishonest site can hold a perfectly valid certificate.

prompt: A user worries that someone on the same network can see which sites they visit. Does a secure connection address that?
optionA: Only partly; the contents are hidden, and which site was contacted is largely not
optionB: Yes, completely; nothing is visible
optionC: No; a secure connection hides nothing on a shared network
optionD: Yes; the site name is encrypted along with everything else
correctAnswerText: Only partly; the contents are hidden, and which site was contacted is largely not
explanation: The contents of the exchange are protected and the fact that a connection was made to a particular host is largely observable. Overstating what encryption covers is as unhelpful as denying it covers anything.

prompt: Data submitted over a secure connection is later found exposed. The connection was genuinely encrypted and no interception occurred. Where is the likely exposure?
optionA: During transmission, which must not have been encrypted after all
optionB: In the browser, which must have kept a copy
optionC: Where the data was stored or handled after arriving, which encryption in transit does not touch
optionD: In the address, which carried the data
correctAnswerText: Where the data was stored or handled after arriving, which encryption in transit does not touch
explanation: Encryption protects the journey, and the stem rules out any failure there. Once the data arrives it is in the clear on the server, which is a separate problem needing separate measures.

prompt: A request that needs identification arrives without any. What does the server do?
optionA: Serves it, because the user is logged in elsewhere
optionB: Refuses it, because it has no way to know who is asking
optionC: Serves it, using the address to identify the user
optionD: Waits for a second request carrying the identification
correctAnswerText: Refuses it, because it has no way to know who is asking
explanation: Each request stands alone, so identification missing from this one is simply missing. Being logged in is a property of what the client sends, not a state the server holds.

prompt: A user is logged in in one browser tab and a request from a second tab is refused as unidentified. Both tabs are open to the same site in the same browser. What explains it?
optionA: The server has logged the user out
optionB: Two tabs cannot share a login
optionC: The second tab is using a different address
optionD: The second request did not carry the identifying data, which travels per request rather than per user
correctAnswerText: The second request did not carry the identifying data, which travels per request rather than per user
explanation: Identity rides on each request, so a request that omits it is anonymous whatever other tabs are doing. Tabs can and normally do share stored identification — this one did not send it.

prompt: A page is requested twice in quick succession. Does the second request necessarily reach the server?
optionA: No; a stored copy of the earlier response may be used instead
optionB: Yes; every request reaches the server
optionC: Yes, unless the server is unavailable
optionD: No; a second identical request is always discarded
correctAnswerText: No; a stored copy of the earlier response may be used instead
explanation: Responses may be kept and reused, which is what makes a second load fast. Whether the server is contacted depends on what the first response said about reuse.

prompt: A user reports that a page shows yesterday's data. The server has today's data and returns it to every request it receives. Where is the problem?
optionA: The server is returning stale data
optionB: The user is looking at the wrong address
optionC: A stored copy is being reused, so the request is not reaching the server
optionD: The data was never updated
correctAnswerText: A stored copy is being reused, so the request is not reaching the server
explanation: The server behaving correctly for every request it receives, combined with a stale page, means some requests are not arriving. Reuse of an earlier response is what produces exactly that.

prompt: A request produces no status at all and no response. What does that suggest?
optionA: The server failed while handling it
optionB: The request never reached a server, so nothing was there to answer it
optionC: The address was wrong
optionD: The response was empty
correctAnswerText: The request never reached a server, so nothing was there to answer it
explanation: A status is produced by a server, so its complete absence points at the request not arriving. A wrong address would have reached a server and been refused with a status.

prompt: A request returns a status saying the resource was not found. The address is confirmed correct and the server is running. What follows?
optionA: The address must be wrong after all
optionB: The server must be down
optionC: The request was malformed
optionD: The address is right and the resource is not there
correctAnswerText: The address is right and the resource is not there
explanation: A not-found status distinguishes a reachable server from a present resource, and the stem confirms both the address and the server. What remains is that nothing exists at that address to return.

prompt: A request returns a success status, and the body contains a message saying the operation failed. Which is true?
optionA: The exchange succeeded and the operation did not; the two are separate outcomes
optionB: The status is wrong and should have reported a failure
optionC: The body is wrong, since the status says success
optionD: Both report the same thing, so the operation succeeded
correctAnswerText: The exchange succeeded and the operation did not; the two are separate outcomes
explanation: A status describes whether the request was received and handled; the body describes what happened. A server can perfectly well succeed in telling you that something did not work.

prompt: Two failures look alike to a user: the request never arrived, and the server refused it. How would you tell them apart, and why does it matter?
optionA: By the time each takes, which is always different
optionB: They cannot be told apart from the client
optionC: By whether a status came back at all; one is worth retrying and one will fail identically every time
optionD: By the address, which differs in each case
correctAnswerText: By whether a status came back at all; one is worth retrying and one will fail identically every time
explanation: A status is produced only by a server, so its presence separates the two. Retrying is sensible for one and futile for the other, which is why the distinction is worth making before acting.

prompt: A request fails intermittently, succeeding about half the time with no change to the request. What class of cause fits, and what does not?
optionA: A wrong address, which sometimes resolves
optionB: Something varying between attempts — load, timing or which server answered; a wrong address would fail every time
optionC: A malformed body, which is sometimes accepted
optionD: Randomness, which needs no further explanation
correctAnswerText: Something varying between attempts — load, timing or which server answered; a wrong address would fail every time
explanation: An unchanging request with varying outcomes means something on the other side varies. Both a wrong address and a malformed body would produce the same refusal on every attempt.

prompt: A server reads a price from a hidden field the page itself set, and charges that amount. The page sets the field correctly and the site works as intended for ordinary users. Is the assumption safe?
optionA: Yes; the page set the value, so it is correct
optionB: Yes, provided the field is hidden from view
optionC: No; but only if the connection is not encrypted
optionD: No; anything in a request can be altered before it is sent, whatever the page set
correctAnswerText: No; anything in a request can be altered before it is sent, whatever the page set
explanation: The page runs on the client, so what it sets is a starting value rather than a guarantee. Encryption protects the journey and does nothing about what was put in before it began.

prompt: A server trusts a header claiming which user is making the request, because its own pages always set that header correctly. Is that safe?
optionA: No; a request can carry any header at all, and the server cannot tell which page it came from
optionB: Yes; the header is set by the server's own pages
optionC: Yes, provided the header name is not documented
optionD: No; but only for requests from other sites
correctAnswerText: No; a request can carry any header at all, and the server cannot tell which page it came from
explanation: Nothing about a request reveals what produced it, so a header is a claim like any other. Being undocumented is obscurity rather than protection.

prompt: A page validates a form before submitting it, and the server accepts whatever arrives. Where is the gap?
optionA: There is no gap; the page validates correctly
optionB: The gap is that validation runs twice, wasting time
optionC: A request need not come from that page at all, so nothing has been validated as far as the server knows
optionD: The gap is that the page may fail to validate some inputs
correctAnswerText: A request need not come from that page at all, so nothing has been validated as far as the server knows
explanation: Client-side validation improves the experience for someone using the page and constrains nothing about what reaches the server. Requests can be made without the page being involved.

prompt: If the server must validate everything anyway, is validating in the page worth doing?
optionA: No; it duplicates work the server must do
optionB: Yes; it gives immediate feedback and saves round trips, and it replaces nothing on the server
optionC: No; it gives users a false sense of security
optionD: Yes; it removes the need for some server checks
correctAnswerText: Yes; it gives immediate feedback and saves round trips, and it replaces nothing on the server
explanation: The two validations serve different purposes: one is about the experience and one is about correctness. Treating the client check as removing server checks is exactly the error, and dropping it costs the user a round trip for every mistake.

prompt: Which parts of a request can a server trust as coming unaltered from its own page?
optionA: The headers, which the browser controls
optionB: The method and address, which the page sets
optionC: Hidden fields, which the user cannot see
optionD: None of them; every part is supplied by the client and can be anything
correctAnswerText: None of them; every part is supplied by the client and can be anything
explanation: The whole request is constructed on the client side, and a request can be built without any page at all. Browsers restrict what a page may do, and nothing restricts what some other tool may send.

prompt: An action must record a payment. Every design below works. Which is the safest to repeat if the client resends it?
optionA: A submitting method carrying an identifier the server uses to recognise a repeat
optionB: A fetch that records the payment when visited
optionC: A submitting method that records a payment each time it arrives
optionD: A fetch that records the payment and returns the receipt
correctAnswerText: A submitting method carrying an identifier the server uses to recognise a repeat
explanation: A request may be resent for reasons outside anybody's control, so the design has to make a repeat harmless. Only one option gives the server a way to recognise that it has already seen this payment.

prompt: An action creates a record. What should the response contain, and why?
optionA: Nothing; the creation is what mattered
optionB: The entire collection, so the caller sees the new state
optionC: A status saying it was created and enough to identify the new record, so the caller can refer to it
optionD: A status only, since the caller made the request
correctAnswerText: A status saying it was created and enough to identify the new record, so the caller can refer to it
explanation: A caller that has just created something almost always needs to refer to it next, and only the server knows the identifier it assigned. Returning the whole collection answers a much larger question at much greater cost.

prompt: One design fetches a large collection and filters it in the browser; another asks the server for the filtered subset. Both display the same thing. What does each cost?
optionA: The first costs nothing, since filtering is fast in the browser
optionB: The first sends far more data and can filter without asking again; the second sends less and needs a request per filter
optionC: The second costs nothing, since less data travels
optionD: They cost the same, since the display is identical
correctAnswerText: The first sends far more data and can filter without asking again; the second sends less and needs a request per filter
explanation: Identical output settles correctness and leaves the traffic pattern entirely open. Which is better depends on how large the collection is and how often the filter changes, so neither is right in general.

prompt: A design puts a state-changing action behind a fetch because it is easier to trigger from a link. What follows, and is the convenience worth it?
optionA: Nothing follows; the method is a matter of style
optionB: The action becomes slower, which is the only cost
optionC: The convenience is worth it, since users click links deliberately
optionD: Anything that follows links can trigger the action; the convenience is real and is not worth an action that fires without being asked
correctAnswerText: Anything that follows links can trigger the action; the convenience is real and is not worth an action that fires without being asked
explanation: The method is a promise to everything that handles the request, and breaking it means the action can be triggered by things that never intended to. Users clicking deliberately is only half of what visits a link.

prompt: A sequence reads x y x y x y. What is the shortest unit that repeats?
optionA: x y x y
optionB: x y
optionC: x
optionD: x y x
correctAnswerText: x y
explanation: Two symbols repeat three times, and no shorter unit does. The four-symbol unit repeats too, which is why the question asks for the shortest.

prompt: A sequence reads p q r p q r p q r. Which unit, repeated, produces it, taken as short as possible?
optionA: p q r p q r
optionB: p q
optionC: p
optionD: p q r
correctAnswerText: p q r
explanation: Three symbols repeat throughout. A two-symbol unit fits the opening and then fails, which is the shape of a unit inferred from the start alone.

prompt: This sequence is built by repeating a single unit: a a b a a b a a b. Taken as short as it can be, what is that unit?
optionA: a a b
optionB: a b
optionC: a a
optionD: a a b a a b
correctAnswerText: a a b
explanation: The unit a a b is three symbols long and includes the doubled opening symbol. Taking a b instead would produce a b a b, which is not what is shown.

prompt: A sequence reads m n n m n n m n n. How long is the shortest repeating unit?
optionA: Two symbols
optionB: Six symbols
optionC: Three symbols
optionD: One symbol
correctAnswerText: Three symbols
explanation: The sequence is built from m n n repeated three times, so the shortest unit is Three symbols long. Six symbols also repeat, being twice the shortest unit rather than the unit itself.

prompt: A sequence reads d e d e d e d. Does it have a repeating unit, and if so what is it?
optionA: No; the sequence does not divide evenly into units
optionB: Yes, d e; the sequence stops part way through a repetition
optionC: Yes, d e d; the last symbol proves the unit is three long
optionD: Yes, d; every symbol is either d or e
correctAnswerText: Yes, d e; the sequence stops part way through a repetition
explanation: A pattern may be cut short without ceasing to be a pattern, so ending mid-unit changes nothing. Reading the trailing d as evidence of a three-symbol unit contradicts the rest of the sequence.

prompt: Is the arrangement a b c b a symmetric, and about what?
optionA: No; the symbols are not all the same
optionB: Yes, about its first symbol
optionC: No; a symmetric arrangement must have an even number of symbols
optionD: Yes, about its middle symbol
correctAnswerText: Yes, about its middle symbol
explanation: Reading it from either end gives the same sequence, with c at the centre. An odd count is perfectly compatible with symmetry — it simply leaves one symbol in the middle.

prompt: Is the arrangement p q p q symmetric?
optionA: No; reading it backwards gives q p q p
optionB: Yes; it repeats regularly
optionC: Yes; it is symmetric about the gap in the middle
optionD: Yes; both halves contain the same symbols
correctAnswerText: No; reading it backwards gives q p q p
explanation: Repetition and symmetry are different properties, and this arrangement has the first without the second. Containing the same symbols in each half is not the same as reading alike in both directions.

prompt: Is the arrangement w x y x w symmetric?
optionA: No; the middle symbol has no partner
optionB: No; five symbols cannot be symmetric
optionC: Yes; the first and last match, and so do the second and fourth
optionD: Yes; every symbol appears twice
correctAnswerText: Yes; the first and last match, and so do the second and fourth
explanation: Symmetry requires each symbol to match its partner counting inward from the ends, and the middle symbol needs none. The symbol y appears once, which is exactly what a centre looks like.

prompt: An arrangement reads r s t s r except that one position has been changed, giving r s t r r. Is it still symmetric?
optionA: Yes; the ends still match
optionB: No; the fourth position no longer matches the second
optionC: Yes; only one position changed
optionD: No; symmetry requires all symbols to differ
correctAnswerText: No; the fourth position no longer matches the second
explanation: Symmetry has to hold at every pair, so a single mismatched position breaks it however much of the rest survives. The ends matching is necessary and not sufficient.

prompt: An arrangement a b c becomes c b a. Which transformation is that?
optionA: A shift
optionB: A repetition
optionC: No transformation; the two are the same
optionD: A mirror
correctAnswerText: A mirror
explanation: A mirror is what reverses the order. A shift would move every symbol along and bring one round to the other end, which gives a different result.

prompt: An arrangement a b c d becomes d a b c. Which transformation is that?
optionA: A shift, with the last symbol brought to the front
optionB: A mirror
optionC: A swap of the two ends
optionD: A sort into reverse order
correctAnswerText: A shift, with the last symbol brought to the front
explanation: Every symbol has moved one place along and the one that fell off the end has come round. Mirroring would have given d c b a, which is not what is shown.

prompt: An arrangement a b c d becomes a c b d. Which transformation is that?
optionA: A mirror
optionB: A shift
optionC: A swap of the two middle symbols
optionD: A half-turn
correctAnswerText: A swap of the two middle symbols
explanation: A swap of the two middle symbols is all that has happened: only those two moved, and they exchanged places. A mirror or a shift would have moved the outer symbols too.

prompt: Someone says an arrangement was mirrored, and someone else says it was given a half-turn. The arrangement is a b b a and both descriptions produce it. What follows?
optionA: One of the two must be wrong
optionB: The two cannot be told apart on this input, because it is symmetric
optionC: A mirror and a half-turn are the same transformation
optionD: The arrangement was not transformed at all
correctAnswerText: The two cannot be told apart on this input, because it is symmetric
explanation: Two different transformations agree on an input that is already symmetric, so this input cannot distinguish them. Testing on an arrangement that is not symmetric is what would settle it.

prompt: A sequence repeats the unit triangle circle, beginning triangle circle triangle circle triangle. What comes next?
optionA: triangle
optionB: square
optionC: The sequence ends here
optionD: circle
correctAnswerText: circle
explanation: Five symbols have been shown and the unit is two long, so the sixth completes the third repetition. Nothing new enters a repeating sequence.

prompt: A sequence repeats the unit a b c. What is at position 10, counting the first symbol as position 0?
optionA: b
optionB: a
optionC: c
optionD: It cannot be found without writing the sequence out
correctAnswerText: b
explanation: Position 10 divided by the unit length of 3 leaves a remainder of 1, and the symbol at that place in the unit is b . Counting from one instead would give a, which is the neighbouring answer.

prompt: Four arrangements: a a b, m m n, p p q, r s s. Which has a different structure?
optionA: a a b
optionB: m m n
optionC: r s s
optionD: p p q
correctAnswerText: r s s
explanation: Three of them double the first symbol and end with a different one; the fourth doubles the second. The letters differ throughout, so only the structure can decide it.

prompt: Four arrangements: x y x, k l k, d e d, f g h. Which has a different structure?
optionA: x y x
optionB: f g h
optionC: k l k
optionD: d e d
correctAnswerText: f g h
explanation: Three arrangements return to their opening symbol and one does not. Every arrangement uses different letters, so content cannot be the discriminator.

prompt: On a two-by-two grid with positions named top-left, top-right, bottom-right, bottom-left, one mark sits at top-left. After a quarter turn clockwise, where is it?
optionA: Bottom-left
optionB: Bottom-right
optionC: Top-left, unchanged
optionD: Top-right
correctAnswerText: Top-right
explanation: A quarter turn clockwise moves each corner to the next one round in that direction. Answering bottom-left turns it the other way.

prompt: On the same grid, marks sit at top-left and bottom-right. After a quarter turn clockwise, where are they?
optionA: Top-right and bottom-left
optionB: Top-left and bottom-right, unchanged
optionC: Bottom-left and top-right, which is a quarter turn the other way
optionD: Top-left and bottom-left
correctAnswerText: Top-right and bottom-left
explanation: Each mark moves to the next corner clockwise, so the pair moves from one diagonal to the other. The second and third options name the same pair of corners, which is why the direction has to be reasoned about rather than recognised.

prompt: A mark at top-left is given a quarter turn clockwise, then another, then another. Someone says three quarter turns leave it where it started. Where is it in fact?
optionA: Top-left, as they said
optionB: Top-right
optionC: Bottom-left
optionD: Bottom-right
correctAnswerText: Bottom-left
explanation: Three quarter turns is a three-quarter turn, which lands one corner short of a full circle. Four would return it to the start, which is what the claim confuses it with.

prompt: A row reads a b c d. It is mirrored about a vertical line down its middle. What does it read afterwards?
optionA: a b c d, unchanged
optionB: d c b a
optionC: b a d c
optionD: d a b c
correctAnswerText: d c b a
explanation: Mirroring about a vertical line exchanges the ends and works inward, reversing the order to give d c b a . Exchanging only adjacent pairs would give b a d c.

prompt: On a two-by-two grid a mark sits at top-left. It is mirrored about a vertical line down the middle. Where is it?
optionA: Bottom-left
optionB: Bottom-right
optionC: Top-left, unchanged
optionD: Top-right
correctAnswerText: Top-right
explanation: A vertical mirror exchanges left and right and leaves top and bottom alone. Answering bottom-left mirrors about a horizontal line instead.

prompt: An arrangement is mirrored about a vertical line, and the result is mirrored about the same line again. Someone expects a different arrangement each time. What is the final result?
optionA: The original arrangement, unchanged
optionB: The mirrored arrangement
optionC: An arrangement mirrored about a horizontal line
optionD: An arrangement turned by a quarter
correctAnswerText: The original arrangement, unchanged
explanation: Mirroring twice about the same line undoes itself, whatever the arrangement was. Expecting each transformation to change things again treats the operations as accumulating when they cancel.

prompt: Facing north, a person turns right. Which direction are they now facing?
optionA: West
optionB: South
optionC: East
optionD: North
correctAnswerText: East
explanation: A right turn from north faces east. Answering west turns the other way, and south would need two turns.

prompt: Starting at a point, a marker moves 3 steps east and then 2 steps west. Where is it relative to where it began?
optionA: 5 steps east
optionB: 1 step east
optionC: 1 step west
optionD: Back where it began
correctAnswerText: 1 step east
explanation: Movements in opposite directions partly cancel, leaving the difference. Adding both distances together ignores the directions entirely.

prompt: Facing north, a marker moves 2 steps forward, turns right, and moves 2 steps forward. Someone says it has moved 4 steps north. The turn happens between the two moves. Where is it?
optionA: 4 steps north
optionB: 4 steps east
optionC: Back where it began
optionD: 2 steps north and 2 steps east of where it began
correctAnswerText: 2 steps north and 2 steps east of where it began
explanation: The turn changes what "forward" means, so the two moves go in different directions. Summing the distances without accounting for the turn is exactly the error the claim makes.

prompt: A sequence reads a a b b a a b b. It has an inner pattern of doubled symbols and an outer pattern alternating between a and b. What comes next?
optionA: a
optionB: b
optionC: a a
optionD: b b
correctAnswerText: a
explanation: The doubled b has just completed, so the outer pattern moves on to a and its first copy comes next. Answering b continues the inner doubling one step too far.

prompt: A sequence reads x y y x y y x. The outer pattern places an x and the inner pattern follows it with two y symbols. What are the next two?
optionA: x y
optionB: y x
optionC: y y
optionD: x x
correctAnswerText: y y
explanation: An x has just been placed, so the inner pattern supplies its two y symbols before the outer pattern comes round again. Continuing the outer pattern first applies the two rules in the wrong order.

prompt: A sequence reads p q q r p q q r. Someone continues it as p q q r p q q r p, which continues the outer pattern. The question asks what comes next at the inner level. What is the answer?
optionA: p, continuing the outer pattern
