optionD: The neighbour has a margin cancelling it
correctAnswerText: Padding grows the element inwards from its edge; moving neighbours away is what margin does
explanation: The element does get larger, so something visibly changed and the neighbour still touches its edge. Which side the padding was applied to would change where the space appeared and not whether the neighbour moved.

prompt: What does the selector .warning target?
optionA: The one element whose identifier is warning
optionB: Every element named warning
optionC: The first element carrying the class warning
optionD: Every element carrying the class warning
correctAnswerText: Every element carrying the class warning
explanation: A leading dot marks a class, which any number of elements may carry. An identifier is marked differently and is meant to appear once.

prompt: What does the selector #total target?
optionA: The element whose identifier is total
optionB: Every element carrying the class total
optionC: Every element named total
optionD: Every element containing the word total
correctAnswerText: The element whose identifier is total
explanation: A leading hash marks an identifier, which is meant to be unique within the page. Swapping the two prefixes is the commonest selector mistake.

prompt: What does the selector nav a target?
optionA: Every navigation element and every link
optionB: Every navigation element that is also a link
optionC: Every link inside a navigation element
optionD: The first link inside a navigation element
correctAnswerText: Every link inside a navigation element
explanation: A space between two selectors means "inside", so the second is looked for within the first. Reading it as two separate selectors would target both kinds of element.

prompt: How does the selector p.note differ from p .note, with a space?
optionA: They are the same; the space is ignored
optionB: The first targets paragraphs carrying the class; the second targets elements with the class inside a paragraph
optionC: The first targets any element with the class inside a paragraph
optionD: The second targets paragraphs carrying the class
correctAnswerText: The first targets paragraphs carrying the class; the second targets elements with the class inside a paragraph
explanation: Without a space the two conditions apply to one element; with a space the second is looked for inside the first. The space is the whole difference and is easy to add or lose by accident.

prompt:
Markup:

A

B

C

. How many elements does .note match?
optionA: One
optionB: Three
optionC: None
optionD: Two
correctAnswerText: Two
explanation: A class selector matches every element carrying the class wherever it appears, so both marked paragraphs match. Assuming a class matches one element confuses it with an identifier.

prompt:
A menu is written as
  • Home
  • About
. Which selector reaches the About entry and nothing else?
optionA: .current
optionB: .item
optionC: #menu li
optionD: li
correctAnswerText: .current
explanation: Only the second entry carries current, so .current isolates it. The other three each reach both entries, because both carry item and both sit inside the menu.

prompt: A colour is set on a container. Do the paragraphs inside it take that colour?
optionA: No; every property must be set on each element
optionB: Only if the paragraphs have no colour of their own and no class
optionC: Yes; colour is one of the properties children inherit
optionD: Only the first paragraph does
correctAnswerText: Yes; colour is one of the properties children inherit
explanation: Text-related properties pass down to children unless something overrides them. A paragraph with its own colour would use that instead, which is different from needing one.

prompt: A border is set on a container. Do the paragraphs inside it get a border?
optionA: Yes; children inherit everything from a parent
optionB: No; a border is not inherited
optionC: Yes; borders inherit in the same way as colour
optionD: Only the paragraphs with no border of their own
correctAnswerText: No; a border is not inherited
explanation: Some properties inherit and others do not, and box properties such as borders are in the second group. Assuming inheritance is all-or-nothing gets one of the two cases wrong whichever way it is assumed.

prompt: Two rules both target the same paragraph with equal specificity: the first sets the colour to red and the second to blue. Which applies?
optionA: Red, because the first rule was applied first
optionB: Neither; the conflict cancels both
optionC: Both, blended together
optionD: Blue, because the later rule wins when specificity is equal
correctAnswerText: Blue, because the later rule wins when specificity is equal
explanation: Order decides only when specificity is level, which it is here. Nothing blends or cancels — one value is used.

prompt: A rule .note { color: red; } appears first, and p { color: blue; } appears after it. A paragraph carries the class note. Which colour applies?
optionA: Red, because the class selector is more specific than the element selector
optionB: Blue, because it appears later
optionC: Blue, because element selectors are stronger
optionD: Neither; the two cancel out
correctAnswerText: Red, because the class selector is more specific than the element selector
explanation: Specificity is considered before order, so a later rule loses to a more specific earlier one. This is the case where "the last rule wins" gives the wrong answer.

prompt: A developer moves a rule to the bottom of the stylesheet to make it win, and the colour does not change. Their rule uses an element selector and the competing rule uses a class. What happened?
optionA: The stylesheet was cached
optionB: The move introduced a syntax error
optionC: The competing rule is more specific, and moving a rule later does not overcome that
optionD: The rule is now too late in the file to apply
correctAnswerText: The competing rule is more specific, and moving a rule later does not overcome that
explanation: Order is only consulted when specificity ties, so a more specific rule wins from anywhere in the file. The move was based on a rule that holds only in the equal-specificity case.

prompt: Which is more specific: p or .note?
optionA: p
optionB: .note
optionC: They are equal
optionD: It depends which appears first
correctAnswerText: .note
explanation: A class outranks an element selector regardless of order. Order is only consulted when the two are level.

prompt: Which is more specific: body div section p, or .note?
optionA: body div section p, since it has four parts
optionB: They are equal
optionC: It depends which appears first
optionD: .note
correctAnswerText: .note
explanation: Specificity compares the kinds of selector rather than how many there are, and one class outranks any number of element selectors. Length is the intuition this case exists to break.

prompt: A developer adds three more element names to their selector to make it beat a class rule, and it still loses. Their selector is now six elements long. Why?
optionA: Element selectors never accumulate into a class's worth of specificity, however many are added
optionB: Six is too many selectors to combine
optionC: The class rule appears later in the file
optionD: The extra elements do not match the markup
correctAnswerText: Element selectors never accumulate into a class's worth of specificity, however many are added
explanation: The comparison is made level by level, and no quantity of the weaker kind reaches the stronger. Adding more of what is already losing cannot change the outcome.

prompt: An element has a content width of 100px and padding of 10px on each side, with no border. How wide is it in total?
optionA: 100px
optionB: 110px
optionC: 120px
optionD: 140px
correctAnswerText: 120px
explanation: Padding is added on both sides, so twice ten is added to the content width. Counting one side only gives 110.

prompt: An element must end up occupying exactly 240px across. It carries padding of 15px on each side and a border of 5px on each side. What content width is needed?
optionA: 240px
optionB: 200px
optionC: 220px
optionD: 210px
correctAnswerText: 200px
explanation: Padding and border are both doubled, so forty of the 240 is taken before the content, leaving 200px. Subtracting only one side of each leaves 220.

prompt: An element has a content width of 100px, padding of 10px each side and a margin of 20px each side. A developer says it occupies 160px. The question asks for the width of the element itself, not the space it reserves. What is it?
optionA: 160px, as they said
optionB: 100px, since padding is inside the content
optionC: 140px, counting the margin on one side
optionD: 120px; the margin is outside the element rather than part of it
correctAnswerText: 120px; the margin is outside the element rather than part of it
explanation: Margin is space around the element and belongs to no element's own width. The 160 answers a different and reasonable question — how much horizontal space is reserved — which is why the stem says which is being asked.

prompt: Two block elements follow one another in the markup. How are they arranged?
optionA: Stacked, one below the other
optionB: Side by side
optionC: Overlapping
optionD: Side by side if there is room
correctAnswerText: Stacked, one below the other
explanation: A block element takes the full width available, so the next one starts on a new line. Sitting side by side is what inline elements do.

prompt: Two inline elements follow one another in the markup. How are they arranged?
optionA: Stacked, one below the other
optionB: Side by side, never wrapping
optionC: Side by side, wrapping to the next line if there is not room
optionD: Overlapping
correctAnswerText: Side by side, wrapping to the next line if there is not room
explanation: Inline elements flow like words in a sentence and wrap when the line runs out. That flow is exactly what distinguishes them from block elements.

prompt: A developer sets a width on an inline element and nothing changes. The rule is being applied and the selector matches. Why is the width ignored?
optionA: The width value is invalid
optionB: An inline element is sized by its content, so a width has no effect on it
optionC: A more specific rule is setting the width
optionD: The element has no content to size
correctAnswerText: An inline element is sized by its content, so a width has no effect on it
explanation: The stem rules out the rule not applying, so the value is reaching the element and doing nothing. Width applies to elements that participate in block layout, which an inline element does not.

prompt: A child element is given a width of 50%. What is that a percentage of?
optionA: The width of the screen
optionB: The width of the whole page
optionC: Its own content width
optionD: Its parent's width
correctAnswerText: Its parent's width
explanation: A percentage width resolves against the containing element. Resolving it against the screen would give the same answer only when the parent happens to fill the screen.

prompt: A container has a font size of 20px and a child is given a font size of 1.5 of the inherited size. What size is the child's text?
optionA: 30px
optionB: 1.5px
optionC: 24px, based on a 16px default
optionD: 20px
correctAnswerText: 30px
explanation: A relative font unit multiplies the size inherited from the parent, which is 20 here. Resolving it against the document default ignores the inheritance.

prompt: A developer sets a font size in pixels and a reader's enlarged text setting has no effect on it. The setting works on the rest of the page. What accounts for it?
optionA: The reader's setting is broken
optionB: The rule is more specific than the reader's setting
optionC: A fixed unit does not scale with the reader's preference, while relative units do
optionD: Pixels are a relative unit and should have scaled
correctAnswerText: A fixed unit does not scale with the reader's preference, while relative units do
explanation: Fixed units mean exactly what they say and ignore the reader's preference, which is the whole difference from relative ones. The rest of the page scaling shows the setting itself is working.

prompt: Three block elements sit inside a container whose display is set to arrange its children in a row. How are they arranged?
optionA: Stacked one below the other, as blocks normally are
optionB: Side by side in a row
optionC: Overlapping at the same position
optionD: Side by side only if each is given a width
correctAnswerText: Side by side in a row
explanation: The container's arrangement governs how its children are laid out, overriding their default block behaviour. Nothing further is needed to place them in a row.

prompt: A container arranges its children in a row, and one child also has a rule stacking its own children below one another. Both rules are valid and both apply. What is the result?
optionA: Everything is stacked
optionB: Everything sits in a row
optionC: The two rules conflict and neither applies
optionD: The children of the container sit in a row, and inside one of them its own children are stacked
correctAnswerText: The children of the container sit in a row, and inside one of them its own children are stacked
explanation: Each container governs only its own children, so the two rules act at different levels and both take effect. Reading them as competing assumes one arrangement applies to the whole page.

prompt: A stylesheet has base rules and a conditional block applying at widths of 600px and above. The screen is 800px wide. Which styles are in effect?
optionA: Both; the conditional block adds to the base rules rather than replacing them
optionB: Only the conditional block
optionC: Only the base rules
optionD: Neither, since the conditions overlap
correctAnswerText: Both; the conditional block adds to the base rules rather than replacing them
explanation: Conditional rules are ordinary rules that apply when their condition holds, so they join the cascade rather than replacing what came before. Anything they do not mention keeps its base value.

prompt: A conditional block applies at widths of 600px and above. The screen is exactly 600px. Does it apply?
optionA: No; the boundary is excluded
optionB: It is undefined at exactly the boundary
optionC: Yes; "and above" includes the boundary value itself
optionD: Only if another condition also holds
correctAnswerText: Yes; "and above" includes the boundary value itself
explanation: The condition includes its endpoint, so the boundary width is covered. This is the same boundary reasoning as any inclusive comparison, and it is where two adjacent conditional blocks can overlap or leave a gap.

prompt: A rule targeting .btn has no effect, and the developer tools show the rule is not listed against the element at all. What is the cause?
optionA: A more specific rule is overriding it
optionB: The selector does not match the element
optionC: The stylesheet is cached
optionD: The property is misspelled
correctAnswerText: The selector does not match the element
explanation: A rule that loses the cascade is still listed against the element, struck through. Not being listed at all means the selector never matched.

prompt: A rule has no effect. The developer tools list it against the element with its value struck through. The selector clearly matches and the file is loading. What is the cause?
optionA: The selector does not match
optionB: The stylesheet failed to load
optionC: The property name is misspelled
optionD: Another rule won the cascade for that property
correctAnswerText: Another rule won the cascade for that property
explanation: Being listed means the selector matched and the file loaded; being struck through means it lost to something else. A misspelled property would be listed as unrecognised rather than overridden.

prompt: Three causes make a style fail to appear: the selector does not match, the rule lost the cascade, or the file did not load. Which single piece of evidence separates them fastest?
optionA: The developer tools' list of rules for that element: absent, struck through, or the whole file missing
optionB: Reloading the page
optionC: Reading the stylesheet again
optionD: Adding the style directly to the element
correctAnswerText: The developer tools' list of rules for that element: absent, struck through, or the whole file missing
explanation: The rules panel distinguishes all three at once, because each cause leaves a different trace. Applying the style directly proves it can work and says nothing about which cause was blocking it.

prompt: A developer fixes a style that would not apply by marking it as most important. It now works. What has that established about the original cause?
optionA: That the selector was wrong
optionB: That the file was not loading
optionC: Only that the rule can win when forced; it does not say why it was losing, or whether it matched before
optionD: That another rule was overriding it
correctAnswerText: Only that the rule can win when forced; it does not say why it was losing, or whether it matched before
explanation: Forcing a rule to win changes the outcome without revealing the cause, and it would not have worked had the selector never matched — so it does narrow things slightly. What it mainly does is close the investigation before the cause is known.

prompt: A style applies on the developer's machine and not for other users. The stylesheet on the server contains the rule. What is the likely cause?
optionA: The selector does not match for other users
optionB: Other users are being served a stored copy of the stylesheet from before the rule was added
optionC: The rule is invalid for other browsers
optionD: The developer's browser is applying an extra rule
correctAnswerText: Other users are being served a stored copy of the stylesheet from before the rule was added
explanation: A split between the developer and everyone else, with the server holding the right file, is what a stored copy produces. The selector and the markup are the same for everybody.

prompt: A style from a library cannot be edited and must be overridden on one component. Every option below would win. Which has the least collateral effect?
optionA: A rule marked as most important, applied to the element type
optionB: A rule targeting the element type across the whole page
optionC: An inline style on every instance of the component
optionD: A rule with a slightly higher specificity, targeting only that component
correctAnswerText: A rule with a slightly higher specificity, targeting only that component
explanation: Winning is not the difficulty; every option does that. What separates them is how much else they touch and how hard they make the next override — marking a rule most important wins and leaves nothing above it.

prompt: An override relies on appearing later in the file than the rule it beats. What is the risk?
optionA: If the load order changes, the override silently stops working
optionB: There is no risk; order is fixed
optionC: The override will apply twice
optionD: The override will affect other elements
correctAnswerText: If the load order changes, the override silently stops working
explanation: Order-based wins depend on something outside the rule itself, and load order is not always under the author's control. An override that wins on specificity does not care when it is loaded.

prompt: Marking a rule as most important wins reliably. Why is it a poor first choice?
optionA: It does not always win
optionB: It is slower to apply
optionC: It leaves nothing stronger for the next override, so the next problem has no clean solution
optionD: It only works on some properties
correctAnswerText: It leaves nothing stronger for the next override, so the next problem has no clean solution
explanation: It works, which is why it is reached for. The cost is paid later, when somebody needs to override the override and the ordinary tools have already been exhausted.

prompt: An override is written with a very long, highly specific selector so that it certainly wins. What does that cost?
optionA: Nothing; specificity is free
optionB: It ties the rule to the current markup, so it stops applying if the structure changes
optionC: It slows the page noticeably
optionD: It affects elements elsewhere on the page
correctAnswerText: It ties the rule to the current markup, so it stops applying if the structure changes
explanation: A long selector describes a path through the document, and every element in it becomes something the rule depends on. Rearranging the markup then breaks styling that has nothing wrong with it.

prompt: What is the general principle behind choosing an override?
optionA: Always win by the largest margin available
optionB: Always rely on order, which is simplest
optionC: Avoid overriding library styles at all
optionD: Win by the smallest margin that is robust, so later changes still have room to work
correctAnswerText: Win by the smallest margin that is robust, so later changes still have room to work
explanation: Every override is followed by another one eventually, and the choice made now decides what is available then. Winning by as much as possible and refusing to override at all are both ways of avoiding the judgement.

prompt: Two rule sets produce an identical page for the markup shown: one targets .note and one targets p. The markup contains exactly one paragraph, which carries the class note. Are they equivalent?
optionA: No; they differ as soon as a paragraph without the class, or a non-paragraph with it, is added
optionB: Yes; the page is identical
optionC: No; they differ in appearance already
optionD: Yes, provided the markup is not changed
correctAnswerText: No; they differ as soon as a paragraph without the class, or a non-paragraph with it, is added
explanation: The two selectors happen to select the same single element here and describe different sets. Equivalence for one document is much weaker than equivalence for the documents it might become.

prompt: Two rules set the same property to the same value and differ only in specificity. Nothing else currently competes for that property. Are they equivalent?
optionA: Yes, always
optionB: No; different specificity always changes the result
optionC: For now yes, and they will differ as soon as another rule competes for the property
optionD: No; the more specific rule renders differently
correctAnswerText: For now yes, and they will differ as soon as another rule competes for the property
explanation: Specificity has no effect until there is a competition, so today the two are indistinguishable. What differs is how each behaves when the stylesheet grows.

prompt: Two stylesheets differ only in the order of two rules that target different, non-overlapping sets of elements. Are they equivalent?
optionA: No; order always matters in a stylesheet
optionB: Yes; order matters only between rules competing for the same property on the same element
optionC: No; the later rule always wins
optionD: Yes, but only if both use the same selector kind
correctAnswerText: Yes; order matters only between rules competing for the same property on the same element
explanation: Two rules that never apply to the same element cannot compete, so their relative order is invisible. Order is a tie-breaker rather than a general property of the file.

prompt: What has to be checked before calling two rule sets equivalent?
optionA: That the page looks the same
optionB: That they contain the same number of rules
optionC: That they use the same properties
optionD: That they agree on the markup shown and on markup the selectors might also match
correctAnswerText: That they agree on the markup shown and on markup the selectors might also match
explanation: A stylesheet describes a set of documents rather than one, so agreement on the present markup is only part of the claim. Two rule sets can look identical today and diverge the moment an element is added.

prompt: An employees table has the headings emp_id, full_name, department, joined_on and holds three employees. What is one employee's entry across all four headings called?
optionA: A column
optionB: A row
optionC: A heading
optionD: A table
correctAnswerText: A row
explanation: One employee's entry across the whole width of the table is a row. It runs across the headings rather than down one of them.

prompt: In that same table, department taken all the way down the table is what?
optionA: A row
optionB: A single value
optionC: A key
optionD: A column
correctAnswerText: A column
explanation: A heading together with everything stored under it is a column. It runs down the table rather than across one employee.

prompt: Printed on paper the employees table shows a line of headings and then three employees. How many rows of data does it hold?
optionA: Three
optionB: Four, counting the headings
optionC: One
optionD: Twelve, one per value
correctAnswerText: Three
explanation: The headings name the columns and are not data, so the table holds three rows. Each employee contributes one.

prompt: The department column holds Sales, Sales and Support. What has to be true of the values in any one column?
optionA: They are all different from each other
optionB: They are always text
optionC: They are all the same kind of thing
optionD: They are stored in alphabetical order
correctAnswerText: They are all the same kind of thing
explanation: A column records one kind of thing about every row, so the values are all the same kind of thing. They may repeat, and they are not kept in any particular order.

prompt: Where in the table is one particular employee's department found?
optionA: Anywhere in the department column
optionB: Where that employee's row meets the department column
optionC: In the line of headings
optionD: In a separate table, since a department is not an employee
correctAnswerText: Where that employee's row meets the department column
explanation: A single stored value sits where a row and a column cross, so it is found where that employee's row meets the department column. Knowing only the column narrows it to a list of departments and not to one.

prompt: A table holds emp_id, full_name, email and date_of_birth. Which column is intended to serve as the key?
optionA: full_name
optionB: date_of_birth
optionC: email
optionD: emp_id
correctAnswerText: emp_id
explanation: The identifier column exists for exactly this purpose, so emp_id is the key. The others describe the employee rather than identify the row.

prompt: Two different employees are both recorded as Ana Kumar. What does that show about full_name?
optionA: It cannot be relied on to identify one row
optionB: It can, as long as the two work in different departments
optionC: It can, because the two rows have different identifiers
optionD: It can, once one of the two names is corrected
correctAnswerText: It cannot be relied on to identify one row
explanation: A value that appears twice picks out two rows rather than one, so the name cannot be relied on to identify one row. Nothing about the rest of the row repairs that.

prompt: What does a column have to do before it can be used as a key?
optionA: Hold numbers rather than text
optionB: Be the first column in the table
optionC: Pick out exactly one row, every time and forever
optionD: Be kept in sorted order
correctAnswerText: Pick out exactly one row, every time and forever
explanation: A key has one job, which is to pick out exactly one row, every time and forever. Its type and its position in the table are irrelevant to that.

prompt: In a table of forty employees, every value in date_of_birth happens to be different. Does that make it a key?
optionA: Yes; all the values being different is what a key needs
optionB: No; being different today does not make a column different in principle
optionC: Yes, as long as the column is never left blank
optionD: No; a key has to be a number
correctAnswerText: No; being different today does not make a column different in principle
explanation: The fortieth employee hired tomorrow may share a birthday with somebody already there, so being different today does not make a column different in principle. A key has to be guaranteed, not observed.

prompt: A column holds values such as 9876543210 and 0801234567. What type should it be given?
optionA: A whole number, since the values are digits
optionB: A decimal number
optionC: A date, since it is a fixed length
optionD: Text, so that a leading zero survives
correctAnswerText: Text, so that a leading zero survives
explanation: These are labels made of digits rather than quantities, and nothing is ever added to them, so the column should be text, so that a leading zero survives. Stored as a number the second value comes back shorter than it went in.

prompt: A column holds values such as 2026-04-01 and 2025-11-30. What type should it be given?
optionA: A date type
optionB: Text, since it contains dashes
optionC: A whole number, with the dashes removed
optionD: A decimal number
correctAnswerText: A date type
explanation: Stored as a date type the values can be compared and ordered as dates and invalid ones are refused. Stored as text, 2026-04-01 and 01/04/2026 would both be accepted and would not compare sensibly.

prompt: A column records whether an employee is currently active. What type should it be given?
optionA: Free text, so any wording can be used
optionB: A whole number counting the days active
optionC: A true or false type
optionD: A date type
correctAnswerText: A true or false type
explanation: There are exactly two states to record, so a true or false type fits. Free text lets Yes, yes, Y and Active all mean the same thing and none of them compare equal.

prompt: A phone column was given a whole-number type. The value 0801234 was stored and reads back as 801234. What happened?
optionA: The column was declared too short for the value
optionB: A number has no leading zero to keep, so it was never stored
optionC: The leading zero was a typing mistake by the operator
optionD: Numbers are rounded when they are stored
correctAnswerText: A number has no leading zero to keep, so it was never stored
explanation: Eight hundred and one thousand two hundred and thirty-four is the same quantity however it is written, so a number has no leading zero to keep, so it was never stored. The type was chosen because the value looked numeric rather than because it was a quantity.

prompt: A table records the customer's address on every one of their orders. The customer moves, and the address is corrected on some of their orders but not all. What is the consequence?
optionA: The table takes up more space than it needs to
optionB: Nothing goes wrong until the older orders are read
optionC: The database refuses the correction
optionD: The table now gives two different answers to the same question
correctAnswerText: The table now gives two different answers to the same question
explanation: Two stored copies now disagree, so the table now gives two different answers to the same question, and nothing in the data says which is right. Space is a side issue next to that.

prompt: While all the copies of that address still agree, why is recording it on every order already a problem?
optionA: Every future change has to reach every copy, and nothing makes sure it does
optionB: It is not a problem while the copies agree
optionC: It makes the table slower to read
optionD: It uses storage that could be saved
correctAnswerText: Every future change has to reach every copy, and nothing makes sure it does
explanation: The fault is designed in before it appears, because every future change has to reach every copy, and nothing makes sure it does. Today's agreement is luck rather than a guarantee.

prompt: authors holds 1 Rao, 2 Bose, 3 Iyer. books holds 10 Tides with author 2, 11 Reef with author 1, 12 Dunes with author 7. Who wrote Tides?
optionA: Rao
optionB: Iyer
optionC: Bose
optionD: It cannot be told from these two tables
correctAnswerText: Bose
explanation: Tides carries the identifier 2, and the author with identifier 2 is Bose. The reference is followed from the book to the author rather than the other way round.

prompt: In those same tables, Dunes refers to author 7 and no author carries that identifier. What does that tell us?
optionA: It refers to the seventh author in the list
optionB: The reference points at a row that does not exist
optionC: It records that the author is unknown
optionD: It refers to the first author, as a default
correctAnswerText: The reference points at a row that does not exist
explanation: A reference means only the row carrying that identifier, and there is no such row, so the reference points at a row that does not exist. It is not a position in the table and not a way of saying unknown.

prompt: One author may write many books, and each book has exactly one author. Which side carries the reference to the other?
optionA: Each author carries the identifiers of their books
optionB: Both sides carry a reference to the other
optionC: Neither; the two are matched on the author's name
optionD: Each book carries the identifier of its author
correctAnswerText: Each book carries the identifier of its author
explanation: A reference can hold one value, so it belongs on the side that has one thing to point at: each book carries the identifier of its author. Putting it on the author would need room for an unknown number of books.

prompt: A student may enrol on many courses, and a course may hold many students. What shape is that relationship?
optionA: Many on both sides
optionB: One student to many courses
optionC: One course to many students
optionD: One student to one course
correctAnswerText: Many on both sides
explanation: Neither side is limited to one, so the relationship is many on both sides. Describing it in one direction only leaves out half of what is true.

prompt: A designer tries to record that enrolment by adding a course column to the student row. What breaks?
optionA: Course names would be repeated across students
optionB: Nothing; a list of courses can be kept in the column
optionC: A student on three courses needs three values where there is room for one
optionD: The student table becomes too wide to print
correctAnswerText: A student on three courses needs three values where there is room for one
explanation: A single column holds one value per row, and the relationship allows many, so a student on three courses needs three values where there is room for one. Recording the pairs in a table of their own is what fits the shape.

prompt: An orders table repeats the customer's name and address on every order. Which split records each fact once?
optionA: An addresses table keyed on the address text, with orders referring to it
optionB: A customers table, with each order referring to a customer
optionC: One orders table for each city
optionD: No split; the repeated values are identical anyway
correctAnswerText: A customers table, with each order referring to a customer
explanation: The repeated facts are facts about a customer, so they belong in a customers table, with each order referring to a customer. Splitting on the address alone keeps two people at one address sharing a row they should not share.

prompt: After that split, in how many places is one customer's address recorded?
optionA: In one place per order, as before
optionB: In both tables, so either can be read on its own
optionC: Nowhere; it has to be worked out from the orders
optionD: In one place, on that customer's row
correctAnswerText: In one place, on that customer's row
explanation: The point of the split is that the fact is stored once, in one place, on that customer's row. Every order reaches it through the reference rather than keeping a copy.

prompt: A designer goes further and splits the address into separate street, city, state and country tables, each with its own identifier. Every answer the system gives stays correct. What does it cost?
optionA: A question as simple as where a customer lives now needs several tables combined
optionB: Nothing; more tables is always the better design
optionC: Addresses can no longer be corrected
optionD: The duplication comes back in a different form
correctAnswerText: A question as simple as where a customer lives now needs several tables combined
explanation: Correctness is not what suffers, which is why the stem says the answers stay right: a question as simple as where a customer lives now needs several tables combined. Splitting stops paying once the fact being separated is not independently repeated.

prompt: A bonus column is left blank both for employees who received no bonus and for employees whose bonus has not been decided yet. What has been lost?
optionA: Nothing; both cases mean the same in the end
optionB: The total, which can no longer be worked out
optionC: The difference between a bonus of nothing and a bonus not yet known
optionD: The order in which the rows were added
correctAnswerText: The difference between a bonus of nothing and a bonus not yet known
explanation: Two different situations were written down the same way, so what is lost is the difference between a bonus of nothing and a bonus not yet known. A recorded zero and a blank say different things and should not be merged.

prompt: Two rows both have nothing recorded in the same column. Are those two blanks equal to each other?
optionA: Yes; both are empty and so both are the same
optionB: No; a blank is not equal to anything, itself included
optionC: Yes, as long as the column holds text
optionD: Only when the two rows were added at the same time
correctAnswerText: No; a blank is not equal to anything, itself included
explanation: A blank stands for a value nobody knows, and two unknowns cannot be declared the same, so a blank is not equal to anything, itself included. This is why blanks have to be asked for specially rather than compared.

prompt: A manager checks a bonus report and says the reported average should equal the reported total divided by the number of employees. It does not. Both figures come from the same column, in which some rows are blank. Why do they disagree?
optionA: The average is rounded and the total is not
optionB: The total skips blanks while the average counts them as zero
optionC: The two figures are taken over different sets of rows
optionD: The average divides by the number of recorded bonuses, not by the number of employees
correctAnswerText: The average divides by the number of recorded bonuses, not by the number of employees
explanation: Both figures skip the blanks, and they differ in what the average then divides by: the average divides by the number of recorded bonuses, not by the number of employees. The manager's arithmetic silently treats every blank as a zero.

prompt: The employees table declares emp_id as its key. A new row is offered carrying an emp_id that already exists. What happens?
optionA: It is refused, because the key has to be unique
optionB: It is accepted, replacing the existing row
optionC: It is accepted, and a fresh identifier is assigned to it
optionD: It is accepted, and both rows are kept
correctAnswerText: It is refused, because the key has to be unique
explanation: A key that appeared twice would identify two rows and stop being a key, so the row is refused, because the key has to be unique. Nothing is overwritten and nothing is renumbered.

prompt: The same table declares that department_id must refer to an existing department. A new row is offered with department_id 99, and no department carries that identifier. What happens?
optionA: It is accepted, and department 99 is created
optionB: It is accepted, with the reference left blank
optionC: It is refused, because the reference points at nothing
optionD: It is accepted, and matched to the nearest existing department
correctAnswerText: It is refused, because the reference points at nothing
explanation: The constraint exists to stop exactly this row from being stored, so it is refused, because the reference points at nothing. A database does not invent the row that was referred to.

prompt: The same table also declares that full_name may not be blank. A row is offered with a fresh emp_id, a department that exists, and full_name left blank. What happens?
optionA: It is accepted, since only keys and references are enforced
optionB: It is refused, because full_name may not be blank
optionC: It is refused, because its blank duplicates another row's blank
optionD: It is accepted, and the blank is stored as empty text
correctAnswerText: It is refused, because full_name may not be blank
explanation: The first two constraints are satisfied and the third is not, so the row is refused, because full_name may not be blank. Two blanks never count as duplicates of each other, so the key constraint is not what stops it.

prompt: Rows were added to a table in a known order. Does reading the table back return them in that order?
optionA: Yes, always
optionB: Yes, unless a row has been deleted since
optionC: Yes, provided the table has a key
optionD: Not unless the reading asks for an order
correctAnswerText: Not unless the reading asks for an order
explanation: A table is a set of rows and keeps no arrival order, so the rows come back in a known order only unless the reading asks for an order. Seeing them arrive in order proves nothing about the next read.

prompt: A report read the table twice and got the rows in the same order both times. Is that order now guaranteed?
optionA: No; an order that was observed is not an order that was promised
optionB: Yes; two identical reads establish it
optionC: Yes, until the next row is added
optionD: Yes, as long as the key is numeric
correctAnswerText: No; an order that was observed is not an order that was promised
explanation: Nothing about reading a table twice creates a rule, so an order that was observed is not an order that was promised. The same read can come back differently after maintenance, a new index or a change in size.

prompt: A program takes the first row it reads to be the oldest record. It is right for eight months and then wrong, and nothing about the program changed in that time. What happened?
optionA: A row was deleted from the table
optionB: The identifier column ran out of values
optionC: The stored order changed, and it had never guaranteed anything about age
optionD: The table grew too large to read in one go
correctAnswerText: The stored order changed, and it had never guaranteed anything about age
explanation: The program depended on something that was true by accident, so the stored order changed, and it had never guaranteed anything about age. Asking for the oldest by date is what makes the answer stable.

prompt: authors holds four rows: Rao, Bose, Iyer and Nair. books holds five rows: two written by Rao, one by Bose, one by Iyer, and one referring to an author identifier that appears nowhere. Matching the two tables on the author reference gives how many rows?
optionA: Five, one for each book
optionB: Four
optionC: Nine, the two tables added
optionD: Twenty, every possible pairing
correctAnswerText: Four
explanation: Each of the four books whose author exists produces one row, and the fifth matches nothing, so four rows come back. Rao contributes two of them because Rao wrote two books.

prompt: Nair appears nowhere in that matched result, although Nair is in the authors table. Why?
optionA: Nair was removed by a condition on the result
optionB: Nair's row is missing its identifier
optionC: The matching dropped the last row of the authors table
optionD: Nair has written no book, and matching keeps only rows that pair up
correctAnswerText: Nair has written no book, and matching keeps only rows that pair up
explanation: Matching produces a row only where the two sides correspond, so Nair has written no book, and matching keeps only rows that pair up. An author with no books and a book with no author drop out for the same reason.

prompt: A report counts employees for each department and the counts add up to more than the number of employees. Every employee belongs to exactly one department. What explains it?
optionA: Something else joined into the report repeats each employee across several rows
optionB: Some employees have no department recorded
optionC: The line of headings is being counted as a row
optionD: Each department is being counted twice
correctAnswerText: Something else joined into the report repeats each employee across several rows
explanation: The stem rules out an employee belonging to two departments, so the extra rows come from elsewhere: something else joined into the report repeats each employee across several rows. An employee with three recorded skills is counted three times.

prompt: A similar report totals fewer employees than the table holds. The report keeps only rows where the department reference matches a department row. What explains the shortfall?
optionA: Some employees are counted twice and the total was corrected
optionB: The count is being rounded down
optionC: Some employees refer to a department that no longer exists and so match nothing
optionD: The departments table holds more rows than it should
correctAnswerText: Some employees refer to a department that no longer exists and so match nothing
explanation: Rows that fail to match are left out entirely rather than reported as unmatched, so some employees refer to a department that no longer exists and so match nothing. Missing employees and repeated employees are opposite symptoms of two different faults.

prompt: A design records only each customer's current balance. Somebody later asks how much that customer spent last month. Can the design answer?
optionA: Yes, by subtracting last month's balance from this month's
optionB: No; the individual amounts were never written down
optionC: Yes, if the balance carries the date it was last changed
optionD: Yes, from the customers table alone
correctAnswerText: No; the individual amounts were never written down
explanation: Only the running figure was kept and every amount that changed it was discarded, so no; the individual amounts were never written down. Last month's balance is not stored either, which is why the subtraction has nothing to work from.

prompt: A design stores a customer's several phone numbers in one column, separated by commas. Every screen in the system displays them correctly. What can the design not do?
optionA: Show the numbers to a user
optionB: Hold more than two numbers in the column
optionC: Be read by a program at all
optionD: Answer a question about one number, such as which customers share a number
correctAnswerText: Answer a question about one number, such as which customers share a number
explanation: Display works because the whole column is shown at once, which is why nothing looks wrong: what it cannot do is answer a question about one number, such as which customers share a number. The database sees one piece of text rather than several values.

prompt: What kind of question can a design never answer, when it records only the state a thing is in now?
optionA: Any question about how that state was arrived at, or what it was before
optionB: Any question about the present state
optionC: Questions that need more than one table
optionD: Questions that need a total rather than a list
correctAnswerText: Any question about how that state was arrived at, or what it was before
explanation: The present is exactly what such a design keeps, and everything else has been thrown away, so it can never answer any question about how that state was arrived at, or what it was before. The question usually arrives long after the design is in use.

prompt: Recording every change as it happens, as well as the value it produced, answers a wider range of later questions. What does it cost?
optionA: Nothing; it is the better design in every respect
optionB: The current value becomes impossible to find
optionC: Many more rows, and the current value now has to be worked out or kept in step separately
optionD: The table can no longer have a key
correctAnswerText: Many more rows, and the current value now has to be worked out or kept in step separately
explanation: The extra questions are paid for with many more rows, and the current value now has to be worked out or kept in step separately. That second copy is itself a duplication that has to be maintained.

prompt: A design is being settled while the questions it will have to answer are still unknown. What is the safer default?
optionA: Record the summaries, since those are what people actually ask for
optionB: Record the facts as they happen, and work summaries out from them later
optionC: Record both the facts and the summaries in the same column
optionD: Postpone the design until the questions are known
correctAnswerText: Record the facts as they happen, and work summaries out from them later
explanation: A summary can always be produced from the facts and the facts can never be recovered from a summary, so record the facts as they happen, and work summaries out from them later. The asymmetry is what makes this the default rather than a preference.

prompt: A monthly report totals the sales for a month in which no sale was made. The report shows a blank where the total should be, and does not fail. What is the reason?
optionA: The report failed and printed nothing
optionB: The whole sales table is empty
optionC: That month was left out of the report
optionD: A total over no rows has no value to report, unless the report supplies one
correctAnswerText: A total over no rows has no value to report, unless the report supplies one
explanation: There was nothing to add, and adding nothing yields no figure at all: a total over no rows has no value to report, unless the report supplies one. The absence of a failure is the clue that this is normal behaviour rather than a fault.

prompt: For that same empty month the report shows a count of 0 next to a blank total, and both figures are correct. What should the reader take from the pair?
optionA: That no sale was recorded at all, rather than sales that came to nothing
optionB: That the report is inconsistent with itself
optionC: That the total failed while the count succeeded
optionD: That the count is wrong and should also be blank
correctAnswerText: That no sale was recorded at all, rather than sales that came to nothing
explanation: The two figures answer different questions and agree with each other: no sale was recorded at all, rather than sales that came to nothing. A zero total would have been the wrong claim to print.

prompt: A list of departments with the number of employees in each leaves out one department entirely. That department currently has nobody in it. Why is it missing?
optionA: It was removed by a condition somewhere in the report
optionB: Its identifier is missing from the departments table
optionC: Matching produces no row at all for a department with nobody to match
optionD: Counts of zero are dropped when the report is formatted
correctAnswerText: Matching produces no row at all for a department with nobody to match
explanation: The report is built by pairing departments with employees, and matching produces no row at all for a department with nobody to match. The department is absent rather than shown as zero.

prompt: How is that empty department made to appear in the list, showing a count of zero?
optionA: Add a placeholder employee to the empty department
optionB: Keep every department, and count only the employees that match each one
optionC: Count the rows of the departments table instead
optionD: Remove the condition that limits which employees are counted
correctAnswerText: Keep every department, and count only the employees that match each one
explanation: The department has to survive the matching before it can be counted, so keep every department, and count only the employees that match each one. The count then comes out as zero rather than as a missing line.

prompt: Rather than change the report, somebody adds one placeholder employee to each empty department so that every department appears. The list now looks right. What does that cost?
optionA: Nothing; the placeholders are ignored by everything else
optionB: The report becomes slower to produce
optionC: The departments table has to be given new identifiers
optionD: The employees table now holds rows describing nobody, and every count of employees is wrong
correctAnswerText: The employees table now holds rows describing nobody, and every count of employees is wrong
explanation: The fix is applied to the data rather than to the report, so the employees table now holds rows describing nobody, and every count of employees is wrong. Every future reader has to know about the placeholders, and eventually one will not.

prompt: Four columns are proposed as the key of a customers table: the email address, the phone number, the full name, and a number the system assigns. All four hold different values in today's data. Which should be chosen?
optionA: The number the system assigns, because nothing outside the system can change it
optionB: The email address, which is unique and already known
optionC: The phone number, which is unique and shorter
optionD: The full name, combined with the city to make it unique
correctAnswerText: The number the system assigns, because nothing outside the system can change it
explanation: Uniqueness today is the one thing all four have, so the choice turns on what happens next: the number the system assigns, because nothing outside the system can change it. The other three belong to the customer, who is entitled to change them.

prompt: The email address was chosen as the key, and a customer now changes their email address. What has to happen?
optionA: Nothing; the change affects only the customer's own row
optionB: The customer has to be recorded again as a new customer
optionC: Every row anywhere that refers to that customer by email has to be found and changed too
optionD: The old address has to be kept forever alongside the new one
correctAnswerText: Every row anywhere that refers to that customer by email has to be found and changed too
explanation: A key is copied into every row that refers to the customer, so every row anywhere that refers to that customer by email has to be found and changed too. Missing one of them silently detaches part of the customer's history.

prompt: The phone number was chosen as the key, and two people in one household share a landline. What happens when the second person is recorded?
optionA: Both rows are stored and the key stops being enforced
optionB: The second row is refused, and the two people cannot both be held in the table
optionC: The second row replaces the first
optionD: The number is stored twice and a warning is issued
correctAnswerText: The second row is refused, and the two people cannot both be held in the table
explanation: The key constraint does exactly what it was declared to do, so the second row is refused, and the two people cannot both be held in the table. A value that is unique for most people is not a key.

prompt: Why is a system-assigned key preferred, even though it stores a value that means nothing to anybody outside the system?
optionA: It takes up less room than an address or a name
optionB: It can be sorted more quickly than text
optionC: It prevents the same person being recorded twice
optionD: It is never asked to change, which is the one property a key needs and real values lack
correctAnswerText: It is never asked to change, which is the one property a key needs and real values lack
explanation: Meaning is not what a key is for: it is never asked to change, which is the one property a key needs and real values lack. It does nothing at all to stop the same person being entered twice, which is a separate problem.

prompt: What does branching make possible that working in a single line of history does not?
optionA: Keeping a spare copy of the project in case of accident
optionB: Carrying unfinished work forward without disturbing the version that already works
optionC: Giving each person on the team a project of their own
optionD: Storing files that are too large to record
correctAnswerText: Carrying unfinished work forward without disturbing the version that already works
explanation: A branch lets half-done work be recorded and returned to, so it allows carrying unfinished work forward without disturbing the version that already works. In one line, unfinished work and working code have to share the same commits.

prompt: Is a branch a copy of the project folder?
optionA: Yes; each branch gets a folder of its own
optionB: Yes, though only the changed files are duplicated
optionC: No; it is a copy of the most recent commit
optionD: No; it is a second line of history over the same folder
correctAnswerText: No; it is a second line of history over the same folder
explanation: There is one folder and one recorded history, so a branch is a second line of history over the same folder. Believing it duplicates the project is what makes branching feel expensive.

prompt: Two features are being built at the same time. What does giving each one a branch achieve?
optionA: Either can be finished and recorded without the other's half-done work coming with it
optionB: Each feature gets a separate backup
optionC: Each feature gets its own shared copy
optionD: The two features are combined automatically when they are done
correctAnswerText: Either can be finished and recorded without the other's half-done work coming with it
explanation: The two sets of commits stay apart until somebody joins them, so either can be finished and recorded without the other's half-done work coming with it. Nothing is combined until a merge is asked for.

prompt: Can work done on a branch be brought back into the main line later?
optionA: No; a branch is a permanent separation
optionB: Only by copying the files across by hand
optionC: Yes; merging is what joins the two histories
optionD: Only if no further commits were made on the main line
correctAnswerText: Yes; merging is what joins the two histories
explanation: Branches are made to be rejoined, and merging is what joins the two histories. Commits made on the main line in the meantime do not prevent it.

prompt: Why is a branch preferred to simply keeping a second copy of the folder while an experiment is tried?
optionA: A branch takes up less room on the disk
optionB: The two histories can be recombined afterwards, which two folders cannot be
optionC: A branch is quicker to switch between
optionD: A branch cannot produce a clash
correctAnswerText: The two histories can be recombined afterwards, which two folders cannot be
explanation: Two folders leave somebody comparing files by hand at the end, whereas the two histories can be recombined afterwards, which two folders cannot be. Space and speed are side effects rather than the reason.

prompt: What is created at the moment a new branch is made?
optionA: A copy of every file in the project
optionB: A new folder alongside the existing one
optionC: A new shared copy of the project
optionD: A name that points at the commit you are currently on
correctAnswerText: A name that points at the commit you are currently on
explanation: Making a branch records a name that points at the commit you are currently on and nothing else. That is why it is instant however large the project is.

prompt: Do the files in the working folder change at the moment a branch is created?
optionA: No; nothing changes until commits are made or another branch is switched to
optionB: Yes; they are reset to the last recorded state
optionC: Yes; a second set of them appears
optionD: Yes; any unrecorded work is cleared away first
correctAnswerText: No; nothing changes until commits are made or another branch is switched to
explanation: Creating a branch is a note about history rather than an operation on files, so nothing changes until commits are made or another branch is switched to. Unrecorded work is left exactly where it was.

prompt: Does creating a branch require a shared copy of the project?
optionA: Yes; branches exist on the shared copy
optionB: Yes, unless the project has never been shared at all
optionC: No; branches are local until somebody sends them
optionD: Only the first branch requires one
correctAnswerText: No; branches are local until somebody sends them
explanation: Branching is a local act like committing, so branches are local until somebody sends them. A project that has never been shared can have as many as it likes.

prompt: A project of 500 files has six branches. How many copies of those files are sitting on the disk?
optionA: Six, one for each branch
optionB: One working folder, plus one recorded history that all six branches read from
optionC: Six, but only of the files that differ between branches
optionD: Three thousand, one set per branch
correctAnswerText: One working folder, plus one recorded history that all six branches read from
explanation: Branches are names into a single recorded history, so there is one working folder, plus one recorded history that all six branches read from. The count of branches has almost no bearing on the size of the project.

prompt: What does a merge produce?
optionA: A third branch holding the work of both
optionB: Two branches that are now identical
optionC: One branch holding whichever work was newer
optionD: One branch that now holds the work of both
correctAnswerText: One branch that now holds the work of both
explanation: Merging joins one line into another, leaving one branch that now holds the work of both. No third branch is created and nothing is chosen on grounds of age.

prompt: A branch called feature is merged into a branch called main. Which of the two changes?
optionA: main only
optionB: Both of them
optionC: feature only
optionD: Neither; a new branch receives the result
correctAnswerText: main only
explanation: A merge has a direction, and the work travels into the branch being merged into, so main only changes. feature is left exactly as it was.

prompt: Does merging a branch remove that branch?
optionA: Yes, as part of the merge
optionB: Yes, once it has no commits left to contribute
optionC: No; it stays exactly where it was
optionD: Yes, as soon as the merge is sent to the shared copy
correctAnswerText: No; it stays exactly where it was
explanation: A merge copies work into another line and leaves the source alone, so the branch stays exactly where it was. Deleting it afterwards is a separate decision somebody makes.

prompt: After feature has been merged into main, which branches hold the feature work?
optionA: main only, because the work moved there
optionB: Both, since main received a copy and feature still has its own
optionC: feature only, until main is sent
optionD: A new branch created by the merge
correctAnswerText: Both, since main received a copy and feature still has its own
explanation: Merging copies rather than moves, so both hold the work: main received a copy and feature still has its own. What feature does not have is anything main gained from elsewhere.

prompt: You switch to a branch called feature and make two commits. Which branch holds them?
optionA: main, because that is the project's real line
optionB: Both, since they are commits to the same project
optionC: Neither, until they are merged somewhere
optionD: feature
correctAnswerText: feature
explanation: Commits land on whichever branch is current at the time, so feature holds them. They reach anywhere else only through a merge.

prompt: The sequence was: on main, commit A; switch to feature, commit B; switch back to main, commit C. Which commits does main hold?
optionA: A and C
optionB: A, B and C
optionC: A only
optionD: B and C
correctAnswerText: A and C
explanation: B was made while feature was current and the other two while main was, so main holds A and C. Switching away and back does not carry work with it.

prompt: A file was added and committed on feature. You switch to main, where that file was never created. What is in the folder?
optionA: The file is still there, since it exists on the disk
optionB: The file is there but empty
optionC: The file is not there, because the folder now shows what main holds
optionD: The switch is refused while that file exists
correctAnswerText: The file is not there, because the folder now shows what main holds
explanation: Switching rewrites the working folder to match the branch being switched to, so the file is not there, because the folder now shows what main holds. The folder always reflects one branch at a time.

prompt: That file has vanished from the folder after the switch. Has the work been lost?
optionA: Yes; switching discarded it
optionB: No; it is recorded on the other branch and reappears on switching back
optionC: Yes, unless it had been sent to the shared copy first
optionD: No; it is still in the folder but hidden from view
correctAnswerText: No; it is recorded on the other branch and reappears on switching back
explanation: Being absent from the folder and being lost are different things: it is recorded on the other branch and reappears on switching back. Only unrecorded work is ever at risk here.

prompt: Three commits are made on feature. What does main hold afterwards?
optionA: The three commits as well
optionB: The newest of the three commits
optionC: Nothing, until it is brought up to date
optionD: Exactly what it held before
correctAnswerText: Exactly what it held before
explanation: Work on one branch has no effect on another, so main holds exactly what it held before. It is older than feature rather than out of date in any broken sense.

prompt: Both branches contain a file called config.txt. The copy on feature is edited and committed. What does the copy on main contain?
optionA: Its own version, unchanged
optionB: The edited version, since the two files share a name
optionC: An empty file, until the branches are merged
optionD: The edited version, marked as coming from another branch
correctAnswerText: Its own version, unchanged
explanation: A shared name does not make a shared file across two lines of history, so the copy on main holds its own version, unchanged. The two versions meet only in a merge.

prompt: A teammate says main is out of date, because feature has newer commits on it. Is anything wrong with main?
optionA: Yes; the newest commits anywhere are the real state of the project
optionB: Yes; main has to be brought up to date before it can be used
optionC: No; main is a different line, and being newer does not make feature authoritative
optionD: No; main will catch up by itself once feature is sent
correctAnswerText: No; main is a different line, and being newer does not make feature authoritative
explanation: Newer and correct are different claims, so nothing is wrong: main is a different line, and being newer does not make feature authoritative. main is precisely the version that was last agreed to work.

prompt: feature changed a.txt and main changed b.txt. feature is merged into main. What does main hold now?
optionA: The change to a.txt only
optionB: Both changes
optionC: The change to b.txt only
optionD: Neither, until somebody settles which is right
correctAnswerText: Both changes
explanation: The two branches touched different files, so main now holds both changes. There is nothing for anybody to choose between.

prompt: Immediately after that merge, what does feature hold?
optionA: Both changes, since the two branches are now joined
optionB: Nothing; its work moved into main
optionC: Both changes, once the merge has been sent
optionD: Its own change only; the merge did not alter it
correctAnswerText: Its own change only; the merge did not alter it
explanation: The merge wrote into main and left the source alone, so feature holds its own change only; the merge did not alter it. Giving feature main's work takes a merge in the other direction.

prompt: A developer working on feature expects to see their teammate's b.txt change and cannot find it. Both changes are present on main. What has happened?
optionA: The merge updated main only, and feature has never been given main's work
optionB: The merge stopped part way through
optionC: The b.txt change was discarded during the merge
optionD: feature has to be sent before it receives anything
correctAnswerText: The merge updated main only, and feature has never been given main's work
explanation: Both changes are on main, which shows the merge worked: the merge updated main only, and feature has never been given main's work. Merging main into feature is what would bring it across.

prompt: main runs c1, then c2, then c3. feature was started from c2 and has c4 and c5 on it. Which commits are on both branches?
optionA: c1, c2 and c3
optionB: All five of them
optionC: c1 and c2
optionD: None of them
correctAnswerText: c1 and c2
explanation: feature was started at c2 and everything up to that point came with it, so c1 and c2 are on both branches. c3 was added to main afterwards.

prompt: From that same pair of branches, which commits exist only on feature?
optionA: c3, c4 and c5
optionB: c4 and c5
optionC: c5 only
optionD: None; every commit is shared
correctAnswerText: c4 and c5
explanation: Only the commits made after the branch was started belong to it alone, so c4 and c5 exist only on feature. c3 belongs only to main, which is a different question.

prompt: A developer says the two branches went their separate ways at c3, because c3 is the newest commit on main. Where did they actually separate?
optionA: At c3, as the developer said
optionB: At c4, the first commit made on feature
optionC: At c1, where the project began
optionD: At c2, the last commit the two branches have in common
correctAnswerText: At c2, the last commit the two branches have in common
explanation: The separation is where the shared history stops, which is at c2, the last commit the two branches have in common. c3 was made on main after the branches had already parted.

prompt: One branch changed a.txt and the other changed b.txt. Does merging them clash?
optionA: No; changes to different files cannot compete
optionB: Yes; any two sets of changes have to be reconciled
optionC: Yes, if the two files sit in the same folder
optionD: Only if the files are large
correctAnswerText: No; changes to different files cannot compete
explanation: A clash needs two candidate versions of the same text, so no; changes to different files cannot compete. The merge completes without anybody being asked anything.

prompt: Both branches changed the same file: one edited the first line and the other edited the last line of a long file. Does merging clash?
optionA: Yes; both branches touched the same file
optionB: Yes; a file can only be changed on one branch at a time
optionC: No; the two edits are in different places in the file
optionD: Only if the two commits were made on the same day
correctAnswerText: No; the two edits are in different places in the file
explanation: Changes are compared region by region rather than file by file, so no; the two edits are in different places in the file. Both edits end up in the merged version.

prompt: Both branches changed the very same line of the very same file, and both changed it to the same text. Does merging clash?
optionA: Yes; the same line was written on both branches
optionB: No; there is nothing to choose between when the two results agree
optionC: Yes; identical edits on one line are the hardest case
optionD: Only if the two commit messages differ
correctAnswerText: No; there is nothing to choose between when the two results agree
explanation: A clash is a question that needs an answer, and the two branches already agree, so no; there is nothing to choose between when the two results agree. What produces a clash is two different texts competing for one place.

prompt: A merge has left a file holding a marked block: an opening marker, a line reading greeting = "Hello", a dividing marker, a line reading greeting = "Hi", and a closing marker. What must the resolved file contain?
optionA: Both greeting lines, with the markers kept as a record of what happened
optionB: Both greeting lines, with the markers taken out
optionC: Neither greeting line, with the markers taken out
optionD: One chosen greeting line, with all three marker lines taken out
correctAnswerText: One chosen greeting line, with all three marker lines taken out
explanation: Resolving means deciding what the file should say, so it must end with one chosen greeting line, with all three marker lines taken out. Keeping both would leave the variable set twice.

prompt: A marked block appears in a list of allowed countries: one branch added India to the list and the other added Kenya, at the same position. Both additions are wanted. What should the resolved list contain?
optionA: India and Kenya, one after the other, with the markers taken out
optionB: India only, with the markers taken out
optionC: Kenya only, since it was added on the branch being merged in
optionD: India and Kenya, with the markers left in to show the history
correctAnswerText: India and Kenya, one after the other, with the markers taken out
explanation: Marked blocks are not always a choice between alternatives, and here the list should hold India and Kenya, one after the other, with the markers taken out. Picking a side would silently drop a wanted entry.

prompt: A file was committed while it still contained the marker lines, and the project now refuses to run. What happened?
optionA: The merge broke the file as it was being written
optionB: The file was resolved while the wrong branch was current
optionC: The clash was recorded rather than settled, so the markers are now part of the file
optionD: The markers are harmless, so the failure has another cause
correctAnswerText: The clash was recorded rather than settled, so the markers are now part of the file
explanation: The markers are ordinary text as far as everything else is concerned, so the clash was recorded rather than settled, and the markers are now part of the file. Whatever reads the file meets lines it cannot make sense of.

prompt: A history splits into two lines after c2 and the two lines come back together at c6. How many lines of work does c6 draw on?
optionA: One
optionB: Two
optionC: Three
optionD: It cannot be told from the shape
correctAnswerText: Two
explanation: A point where two lines rejoin draws on both of them, so c6 draws on two. The split at c2 and the join at c6 are the two ends of the same pair of lines.

prompt: Somebody reads that shape as a single top-to-bottom sequence and concludes that c4 must have been written after c5. What have they missed?
optionA: The listing is printed with the oldest entry first
optionB: c4 and c5 were both made on the same branch
optionC: The point where the lines rejoined is where they had separated
optionD: The two lines ran alongside each other, so their commits are not in one single order
correctAnswerText: The two lines ran alongside each other, so their commits are not in one single order
explanation: A merged history is not a queue, so the two lines ran alongside each other, and their commits are not in one single order. c4 and c5 may have been written on the same afternoon by two people.

prompt: Yesterday's work does not appear on main. It does appear on feature, where the commits were made. What happened?
optionA: The work was committed onto the branch that was current at the time, which was not main
optionB: The work was lost when the branch was switched
optionC: main was reset to an earlier state
optionD: The work was never committed at all
correctAnswerText: The work was committed onto the branch that was current at the time, which was not main
explanation: The commits exist and they exist somewhere specific, so the work was committed onto the branch that was current at the time, which was not main. Merging is what puts it where it was wanted.

prompt: A file you wrote is not in the folder, the history of the current branch never mentions it, and a colleague can see it listed on another branch. What is the situation?
optionA: The work was deleted and will have to be written again
optionB: The shared copy has not been brought down recently enough
optionC: The work exists on that other branch, and this branch has simply never had it
optionD: The file was added to the ignore list by mistake
correctAnswerText: The work exists on that other branch, and this branch has simply never had it
explanation: A colleague seeing it on a branch settles that it was recorded, so the work exists on that other branch, and this branch has simply never had it. Nothing has been deleted and nothing needs fetching.

prompt: The export feature is finished and committed on a branch of its own, and it does not appear on main. What was not done?
optionA: The export work was never committed
optionB: The export branch was never merged into main
optionC: main was never sent to the shared copy
optionD: The export branch was deleted before it could be used
correctAnswerText: The export branch was never merged into main
explanation: The work is recorded and it is recorded elsewhere, so the export branch was never merged into main. Everything up to the merge was done.

prompt: main has been sent to the shared copy and the export feature still does not appear there. The export branch is itself committed and sent. What is missing?
optionA: The export commits, which were never made
optionB: A second send of the export branch
optionC: A fetch by whoever is looking at the shared copy
optionD: The merge; sending a branch does not put its work into another branch
correctAnswerText: The merge; sending a branch does not put its work into another branch
explanation: Both branches reached the shared copy and neither contains the other's work, so what is missing is the merge; sending a branch does not put its work into another branch. Sending and merging solve different problems.

prompt: Three branches were finished and only two of the three appear in main. Which check identifies the one that was left out?
optionA: Ask which branches have already been merged into main, rather than which branches have commits
optionB: Look at the newest commit message on main
optionC: Check that each of the three branches was sent to the shared copy
optionD: Compare how many commits each branch contains
correctAnswerText: Ask which branches have already been merged into main, rather than which branches have commits
explanation: Every branch has commits, so the presence of commits separates nothing: ask which branches have already been merged into main, rather than which branches have commits. Sending is irrelevant to whether main contains the work.

prompt: To be safe, somebody merges all three branches into main again. Two of them had already been merged. What happens to those two?
optionA: Their work is duplicated in the files
optionB: The merge is refused because they were merged once already
optionC: Nothing changes, because a merge that brings nothing new is not an error
optionD: Their earlier merges are undone and redone
correctAnswerText: Nothing changes, because a merge that brings nothing new is not an error
explanation: A merge brings across whatever the target does not already have, and here that is nothing, so nothing changes: a merge that brings nothing new is not an error. It is a safe thing to do and a poor way to find out what was missing.

prompt: A feature appears on the shared copy's main and not on your main. Both are called main. What is the explanation?
optionA: The feature was never merged into main at all
