explanation: A number is copied when it is assigned rather than shared, so x holds 1 and y holds 5. This is where numbers behave unlike arrays and objects.

prompt: const settings = { theme: "dark" }; settings.theme = "light"; The assignment succeeds and the theme becomes light. Why did const not prevent it?
optionA: const only restricts numbers and strings
optionB: The object was copied before the assignment
optionC: const fixes what the name points at, not the contents of what it points at
optionD: const is only enforced when the file first loads
correctAnswerText: const fixes what the name points at, not the contents of what it points at
explanation: The name still points at the same object afterwards, so nothing const guards has changed: it fixes what the name points at, not the contents of what it points at. Assigning a different object to settings would fail.

prompt: let total = 0; for (let i = 1; i <= 4; i++) { if (i % 2 === 0) total += i; } console.log(total); What is printed?
explanation: Only the even values 2 and 4 are added, giving 6. Adding every value would give ten and adding the odd ones would give four.

prompt: A loop builds text with s = s + i, starting from an empty s. It is meant to produce 123 and produces 012 instead. The loop header is for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++). Which single change fixes it?
optionA: Change s = s + i to s += i
optionB: Keep i starting at 0 and continue while i is not above 3
optionC: Move the printing inside the loop
optionD: Start i at 1 and continue while i is not above 3
correctAnswerText: Start i at 1 and continue while i is not above 3
explanation: The body is right and the range is wrong, so it has to start one later and end one later: start i at 1 and continue while i is not above 3. Changing only the end would give 0123.

prompt: function avg(nums) { let t = 0; for (const n of nums) t += n; return nums.length / t; } The call avg([2, 4]) gives about 0.33 rather than 3. What is wrong?
optionA: The division is the wrong way round; the total should be divided by the count
optionB: The loop never runs
optionC: The total should start at 1 rather than 0
optionD: The values were added as text
correctAnswerText: The division is the wrong way round; the total should be divided by the count
explanation: Six divided by two is three, and two divided by six is what was seen, so the division is the wrong way round; the total should be divided by the count. The loop itself is correct.

prompt: Three things happen while a program runs: one value prints as undefined, one line throws an error, and one total comes out quietly wrong. Which of them stops the program where it happens?
optionA: Only the value that prints as undefined
optionB: Only the total that is quietly wrong
optionC: Only the line that throws
optionD: All three of them
correctAnswerText: Only the line that throws
explanation: A value that prints as undefined and a total that is wrong both let the program continue, which is what makes them hard to notice. Only the line that throws halts it at that point.

prompt: Two values read from input fields are added. Entering 10 and 5 produces 105 rather than 15. Where does the fault lie?
optionA: The addition operator was written incorrectly
optionB: The values arrived as text, so plus joined them instead of adding
optionC: The values were too large to add
optionD: One of the fields was left empty
correctAnswerText: The values arrived as text, so plus joined them instead of adding
explanation: Joining is what plus does when either side is text, and the result is the two entries end to end: the values arrived as text, so plus joined them instead of adding. Converting each value before adding fixes it.

prompt: A loop adds each number in a list to a running total. Every value in the list is a number, and the final total is text. The running total was started as an empty string. What happened?
optionA: One of the values in the list was text after all
optionB: The values were never converted before being added
optionC: The loop ran one time too many
optionD: The total began as text, so every addition joined rather than added
correctAnswerText: The total began as text, so every addition joined rather than added
explanation: The stem says every value is a number, so the text can only have come from the starting value: the total began as text, so every addition joined rather than added. Starting it at 0 fixes it.

prompt: A total came out joined rather than added, because the running total began as text. Which single check would have caught it earliest?
optionA: Printing the type of the running total before the loop starts
optionB: Printing the final total
optionC: Comparing the final total against the expected number
optionD: Converting the final total to a number at the end
correctAnswerText: Printing the type of the running total before the loop starts
explanation: The fault exists before the first addition, so it is visible before the loop: printing the type of the running total before the loop starts finds it immediately. Every other check waits until the damage is complete and then only shows that something is wrong.

prompt: Every entry in a list is converted with Number() before being added. One entry is an empty string. What does that entry contribute to the total?
optionA: Nothing, because it is skipped
optionB: It makes the whole total not a number
optionC: 0, because an empty string converts to zero
optionD: It is joined onto the total as text
correctAnswerText: 0, because an empty string converts to zero
explanation: An empty string converts cleanly rather than failing, so it contributes 0, because an empty string converts to zero. A value such as "abc" is the one that would spoil the total instead.

prompt: Values can be converted to numbers as soon as they arrive, or only at the point where arithmetic happens. What does converting on arrival cost?
optionA: Nothing; it is better in every way
optionB: It forces a decision at the boundary about what an unconvertible value means
optionC: It makes the program noticeably slower
optionD: It makes the original text impossible to keep
correctAnswerText: It forces a decision at the boundary about what an unconvertible value means
explanation: Converting on arrival gains one place to check and one kind of value inside the program, and the price is paid at that boundary: it forces a decision about what an unconvertible value means, right where the program may not yet know what to do about it.

prompt: function sum(nums) { let t = 0; for (const n of nums) t += n; return t; } The call sum([]) finishes without an error. What does it return?
optionA: undefined
optionB: An empty array
optionC: Nothing at all
explanation: The loop body never runs, so the starting value is handed back untouched and the call returns 0. That is why a sum needs no special case for an empty list.

prompt: The same summing function is changed into an average by dividing by nums.length before returning. What does an empty list now produce?
optionA: Not a number, because zero is divided by zero
optionB: 0, exactly as the sum did
optionC: An error that stops the program
optionD: undefined
correctAnswerText: Not a number, because zero is divided by zero
explanation: Both the total and the count are zero for an empty list, so the result is not a number, because zero is divided by zero. The sum survived the empty list and the average does not, which is why the division is the line that needs guarding.

prompt: A greeting is built from user.name. It is called with an object that has no name property, and nothing crashes. What appears in the greeting?
optionA: The greeting is skipped entirely
optionB: An empty gap, with nothing where the name should be
optionC: The word undefined, where the name should be
optionD: An error message in place of the name
correctAnswerText: The word undefined, where the name should be
explanation: A missing property reads as undefined rather than failing, and joining that into text spells it out, so the word undefined appears where the name should be. This is why a missing value often reaches the user rather than the developer.

prompt: Two operations are applied to the same list: summing it, and finding its largest value. Which of the two needs a decision made about the empty case?
optionA: Summing, because there is nothing to start from
optionB: Finding the largest, because there is no value to hand back
optionC: Both, in exactly the same way
optionD: Neither; both are defined for an empty list
correctAnswerText: Finding the largest, because there is no value to hand back
explanation: A sum has a natural answer for an empty list, which is zero, and a largest value has none, so it is finding the largest, because there is no value to hand back, that needs the decision. The author has to choose between an error and a stand-in value.

prompt: An empty list can be handled by returning early at the top of the function, or by letting the ordinary code run and produce the right answer by itself. What does the early return cost?
optionA: Nothing; an early return is always the safer choice
optionB: Noticeably slower running on long lists
optionC: The ability to handle non-empty lists in the same function
optionD: A second path through the function that has to stay correct as the first one changes
correctAnswerText: A second path through the function that has to stay correct as the first one changes
explanation: Where the ordinary code already gives the right answer, the guard adds a second path through the function that has to stay correct as the first one changes. The guard earns its place only when the ordinary code would be wrong.

prompt: One fragment tests if (x) and another tests if (x !== undefined). They behaved identically on every value tried, all of which were non-empty strings. Are they equivalent?
optionA: No; they part company on 0, on the empty string and on null
optionB: Yes; both ask whether x has a value
optionC: No; the second one fails when x is a number
optionD: Yes; undefined is the only value that counts as false
correctAnswerText: No; they part company on 0, on the empty string and on null
explanation: Every value tried counts as true and is also not undefined, so the trials could not separate them. They part company on 0, on the empty string and on null, each of which is present but counts as false.

prompt: Two checks are written: x == null and x === null. Which input separates them?
optionA: null, which only the second matches
optionB: 0, which only the first matches
optionC: undefined, which the first matches and the second does not
optionD: No input separates them
correctAnswerText: undefined, which the first matches and the second does not
explanation: The converting form treats the two empty values as equal, so undefined, which the first matches and the second does not, is the separating input. Every other value is treated the same way by both.

prompt: Two fragments differ only in that one computes a + b and the other computes Number(a) + Number(b). They agreed on every pair of numbers tried. Are they equivalent?
optionA: Yes; converting a number changes nothing about it
optionB: No; they differ as soon as either value arrives as text
optionC: No; the second one fails when given numbers
optionD: Yes, since both give a number in every case
correctAnswerText: No; they differ as soon as either value arrives as text
explanation: Converting a number leaves it alone, which is why the trials agreed, but they differ as soon as either value arrives as text: one joins and the other adds. Numbers were the only inputs that could not tell them apart.

prompt: A colleague says two fragments are interchangeable because the tests pass. What would make the claim stronger?
optionA: Adding more tests of the same kind
optionB: Showing the two produce identical output for one typical input
optionC: Showing the two are the same length
optionD: Naming the inputs that could separate them and showing the two agree on those
correctAnswerText: Naming the inputs that could separate them and showing the two agree on those
explanation: Passing tests only shows the inputs tried did not separate them, and the interesting inputs are the ones nobody thought to try. Naming the inputs that could separate them and showing the two agree on those turns a hope into an argument.

prompt: What is the page tree that scripts work with?
optionA: The file that was delivered from the server
optionB: The browser's live in-memory representation of the page
optionC: A browser option that has to be switched on
optionD: Something supplied by a framework
correctAnswerText: The browser's live in-memory representation of the page
explanation: Scripts work on the browser's live in-memory representation of the page, which the browser keeps for as long as the page is open. The delivered file is only what it was built from.

prompt: Where does that tree come from?
optionA: It is downloaded from the server as a second file
optionB: The developer writes it alongside the markup
optionC: It is created only when a script first asks for it
optionD: The browser builds it from the delivered markup
correctAnswerText: The browser builds it from the delivered markup
explanation: The browser builds it from the delivered markup as the page is read, before any script runs. Nothing extra is fetched and nothing has to be requested.

prompt: Once a page has finished loading, can that tree still be changed?
optionA: Yes, for as long as the page stays open
optionB: No; it is fixed until the page is reloaded
optionC: No; it can be read but never changed
optionD: Only while the page is still loading
correctAnswerText: Yes, for as long as the page stays open
explanation: The tree stays available and changeable for as long as the page stays open, which is what makes interactive pages possible at all. Loading finishing is not a freeze.

prompt: Does a plain script on a page need a library before it can reach the page tree?
optionA: Yes; a library is required
optionB: Yes, unless a framework is used instead
optionC: No; reaching it is part of the browser itself
optionD: Only for changing it, not for reading it
correctAnswerText: No; reaching it is part of the browser itself
explanation: Reaching the tree is part of the browser itself, so a plain script can already read and change it. Libraries make the same work shorter to write rather than possible.

prompt: A script inserts a new paragraph into the page. The developer then asks the browser to show the page source. Is the new paragraph in what they see?
optionA: Yes; the source is kept in step with the page
optionB: No; the source shown is the delivered file, which the script never touched
optionC: Yes, but only after the page is reloaded
optionD: No; the paragraph was never really added
correctAnswerText: No; the source shown is the delivered file, which the script never touched
explanation: The paragraph is genuinely in the live page and not in the delivered file, so the source shown is the delivered file, which the script never touched. Inspecting the live tree shows the paragraph; viewing the source does not.

prompt: A lookup by identifier finds a matching element. What does the lookup produce?
optionA: A collection containing that one element
optionB: The text inside that element
optionC: True, to say it was found
optionD: That one element
correctAnswerText: That one element
explanation: A lookup by identifier produces that one element, ready to be read or changed directly. No collection is involved, so no position has to be taken from it.

prompt: A lookup for every element carrying a class matches three elements. What does the lookup produce?
optionA: A collection of the three elements
optionB: The first of the three elements
optionC: The three elements joined into one piece of text
optionD: The number of matches
correctAnswerText: A collection of the three elements
explanation: A lookup for every match produces a collection of the three elements, whatever the number of matches turns out to be. Reaching any one of them means taking it out of the collection first.

prompt: A lookup by identifier matches nothing. What happens?
optionA: It throws an error and the program stops
optionB: It produces an empty collection
optionC: It produces null and the program carries on
optionD: It produces the closest matching element instead
correctAnswerText: It produces null and the program carries on
explanation: A failed lookup produces null and the program carries on, which is why the failure is only noticed on the next line. Nothing is raised at the lookup itself.

prompt: One lookup asks for a single element and another asks for every match. Neither finds anything. How do the two results differ?
optionA: Both give null
optionB: The single lookup gives null and the every-match lookup gives an empty collection
optionC: Both give an empty collection
optionD: Both raise the same error
correctAnswerText: The single lookup gives null and the every-match lookup gives an empty collection
explanation: The two failures are shaped differently: the single lookup gives null and the every-match lookup gives an empty collection. That is why one crashes on the next line and the other quietly loops zero times.

prompt: A click handler is attached while the page is loading. Has the code inside it run at that point?
optionA: Yes; attaching runs it once
optionB: Yes, and it will also run on each click
optionC: Only once the page has been reloaded
optionD: No; it runs when a click happens
correctAnswerText: No; it runs when a click happens
explanation: Attaching only records what should happen later, so the code inside runs when a click happens and not before. Nothing about the attaching itself executes the body.

prompt: A button carrying one handler is clicked three times. How many times does the handler run?
optionA: Three times
optionB: Once, after which it stops listening
optionC: Once per page load, however many clicks occur
optionD: Never, unless it is attached again after each click
correctAnswerText: Three times
explanation: A handler stays attached and answers every click, so it runs three times. Nothing detaches it after the first.

prompt: A handler is attached and the user never clicks the element. What becomes of the code inside it?
optionA: It runs once when the page finishes loading
optionB: It runs when the user leaves the page
optionC: It never runs
optionD: It runs after a short delay
correctAnswerText: It never runs
explanation: Code inside a handler waits for its event and nothing else triggers it, so it never runs. There is no fallback moment at which it is executed anyway.

prompt: A script attaches a click handler and then prints a line. The user clicks a second later. In what order do the printing and the handler run?
optionA: The handler first, because handlers take priority
optionB: The printing first, because attaching does not wait for anything
optionC: They run at the same moment
optionD: The printing is held back until the click arrives
correctAnswerText: The printing first, because attaching does not wait for anything
explanation: Attaching finishes immediately and the script continues, so the printing happens first, because attaching does not wait for anything. The handler runs a second later when the click actually arrives.

prompt:
The page contains

A

B

. A lookup asks for a single element matching .note. Which is produced?
optionA: The paragraph containing B, as the last match
optionB: Both paragraphs, as a collection
optionC: null, because more than one element matches
optionD: The paragraph containing A
correctAnswerText: The paragraph containing A
explanation: A single-element lookup takes the first match in document order, which is the paragraph containing A. Extra matches are ignored rather than causing a failure.

prompt:
The page contains
X
followed by Y. A lookup asks for every element matching #box .tag. How many are found, and which?
optionA: One: the span containing X
optionB: Two: both spans
optionC: One: the span containing Y
optionD: None, because the span is not a direct child
correctAnswerText: One: the span containing X
explanation: The lookup is limited to what sits inside the identified element, so it finds one: the span containing X. The second span carries the same class but sits outside.

prompt:
The page contains

Hello there

. What does reading the paragraph's text produce?
optionA: Hello there
optionB: Hello
optionC: Hello there
optionD: there
correctAnswerText: Hello there
explanation: Reading the text gives the words with the tags stripped out and the nested words kept, which is Hello there. The nested element contributes its words but not its tags.

prompt:
The page contains
  • Price: 99
    • . What does reading the item's markup produce?
optionA: Price: 99
optionB: Price: 99
optionC: Price:
optionD: • Price: 99
correctAnswerText: Price: 99
explanation: Reading the markup gives everything between the opening and closing tags exactly as it stands, which is Price: 99. The element's own tags are not part of what is inside it.

prompt: A script sets a heading's text to Welcome. Who sees the change?
optionA: Everyone who loads the page from now on
optionB: Everyone, once the server has caught up
optionC: Nobody, until the change is saved
optionD: Only this visitor, in this browser, on this open page
correctAnswerText: Only this visitor, in this browser, on this open page
explanation: The change is made to the copy of the page held in one browser, so only this visitor, in this browser, on this open page sees it. Nothing was sent anywhere.

prompt: After a script has changed a heading, the visitor reloads the page. What heading appears?
optionA: The original one, because the page is built again from the delivered markup
optionB: The changed one, which survives reloads
optionC: No heading at all
optionD: The changed one, until the browser cache is cleared
correctAnswerText: The original one, because the page is built again from the delivered markup
explanation: A reload throws the live tree away and builds a new one, so the original one appears, because the page is built again from the delivered markup. The script would have to run again to change it again.

prompt: A student is sure their form saves data, because after clicking Save the entered values are still on the screen. Their Save handler only writes the values into the page. They reload and everything is gone. What does the reload demonstrate?
optionA: That the save worked but the server has not caught up
optionB: That reloading deleted what had been saved
optionC: That nothing ever left the browser; only the live page had been changed
optionD: That the browser cache was cleared at the wrong moment
correctAnswerText: That nothing ever left the browser; only the live page had been changed
explanation: Values staying on screen prove only that the live page holds them, and the reload rebuilds the page from the delivered markup: nothing ever left the browser; only the live page had been changed. Saving requires sending the values somewhere that outlives the page.

prompt: A stylesheet contains .hidden { display: none; }. A script adds the class hidden to a paragraph that is currently on screen. What happens to it?
optionA: It stays, because the sheet had already been applied when the script ran
optionB: It disappears from view
optionC: It disappears once the page is reloaded
optionD: It stays, because a script cannot bring a sheet rule into play
correctAnswerText: It disappears from view
explanation: Which rules match is worked out again every time the page changes, so the paragraph now matches and It disappears from view. Sheets are not applied once at the start and then forgotten.

prompt: A stylesheet contains #save { color: red; } and .btn { color: blue; }. A script adds the class btn to the element whose identifier is save. What colour is the element?
optionA: Blue, because the class was added most recently
optionB: Blue, because a change made by a script outranks the stylesheet
optionC: Neither; the two rules cancel each other
optionD: Red, because the identifier rule is the more specific of the two
correctAnswerText: Red, because the identifier rule is the more specific of the two
explanation: The element now matches both rules and the cascade settles it on specificity, so it stays red, because the identifier rule is the more specific of the two. When the class was added makes no difference.

prompt: A stylesheet sets an element's colour to red through its identifier. A script sets the colour to green on the element itself. The element shows green, even though an identifier rule is highly specific. Why?
optionA: A style set on the element itself is considered after every stylesheet rule
optionB: Because the script ran later in time than the stylesheet
optionC: Because a script always overrides a stylesheet
optionD: Because green is applied to the text and red to the background
correctAnswerText: A style set on the element itself is considered after every stylesheet rule
explanation: What the script produced is not another stylesheet rule but a style on the element, and a style set on the element itself is considered after every stylesheet rule. Running later is not the reason: a stylesheet loaded afterwards would still lose.

prompt: Three buttons each receive their own handler, and each handler hides the element that was clicked. The second button is clicked. What happens?
optionA: All three buttons are hidden
optionB: The first button is hidden
optionC: The second button is hidden
optionD: Nothing happens
correctAnswerText: The second button is hidden
explanation: Each handler acts on whatever was clicked, so the second button is hidden and the others are untouched. The click decides the target.

prompt: Three similar buttons exist, but a handler was attached to the first one only. The third button is clicked. What happens?
optionA: The first button is hidden
optionB: Nothing, because the third button has no handler
optionC: The third button is hidden
optionD: All three buttons are hidden
correctAnswerText: Nothing, because the third button has no handler
explanation: A handler only answers clicks on the element it was attached to, so nothing happens, because the third button has no handler. Attaching to one element does not cover its lookalikes.

prompt: Every button in a list has a handler attached, and clicking any of them always hides the first button. What is the fault?
optionA: Only the first button actually received a handler
optionB: The handlers were attached before the buttons existed
optionC: All the buttons share one identifier
optionD: The handler acts on a fixed element instead of the one that was clicked
correctAnswerText: The handler acts on a fixed element instead of the one that was clicked
explanation: Something happens on every click, so every button really is wired up and the attaching timing is fine; what is wrong is that the handler acts on a fixed element instead of the one that was clicked. The handler needs the clicked element rather than a name resolved once.

prompt: A script is placed above the markup it looks up and runs as soon as it is reached. Does the lookup find the element?
optionA: No; that part of the page has not been built yet
optionB: Yes; the browser waits for the whole page first
optionC: Yes; lookups search the delivered file rather than the page
optionD: Only when the lookup uses an identifier
correctAnswerText: No; that part of the page has not been built yet
explanation: The page is built from the top downwards and the script runs where it sits, so no, that part of the page has not been built yet. The lookup searches the live tree, which is still incomplete.

prompt: The same script is moved below the markup it looks up. Does the lookup find the element now?
optionA: No; where a script sits makes no difference
optionB: Only after the page is reloaded once
optionC: Yes; the element has been built by the time the script runs
optionD: Only if it also waits for the page to finish loading
correctAnswerText: Yes; the element has been built by the time the script runs
explanation: Everything above a script exists before the script runs, so yes, the element has been built by the time the script runs. Waiting for a load event is another way to get the same guarantee, not a further requirement.

prompt: A lookup gives null when the page loads. Typing exactly the same lookup into the console afterwards finds the element. What is the cause?
optionA: The selector does not match the element
optionB: The script ran before that element had been built
optionC: The element is hidden by a stylesheet rule
optionD: The browser does not support that kind of lookup
correctAnswerText: The script ran before that element had been built
explanation: The console result proves the selector matches and the element exists, so the only thing that differs between the two attempts is when they happened: the script ran before that element had been built.

prompt: A lookup returns the three elements carrying a class. The script then sets a style on the returned collection itself. What happens on the page?
optionA: All three elements change
optionB: The first element changes
optionC: An error stops the script
optionD: Nothing changes
correctAnswerText: Nothing changes
explanation: A collection is a list of elements and not an element, so setting a style on it changes nothing on the page. No error is raised either, which is what makes this hard to spot.

prompt: How is a style applied to every element in such a collection?
optionA: By going through the collection and setting the style on each element in turn
optionB: By setting the style on the collection once
optionC: By setting the style on the first element, which the rest follow
optionD: By running the lookup again for each element
correctAnswerText: By going through the collection and setting the style on each element in turn
explanation: The collection holds the elements but is not one of them, so the work is done by going through the collection and setting the style on each element in turn. There is no shortcut that reaches them all at once.

prompt: A script sets a style on a collection and nothing changes, with no error reported. A colleague says the selector must be wrong. What single check settles which of the two it is?
optionA: Reload the page and try again
optionB: Set the style on the first element instead
optionC: Print how many elements the collection holds
optionD: Try a different style property
correctAnswerText: Print how many elements the collection holds
explanation: A wrong selector and a style set on the collection look identical from outside, and they differ in exactly one observable: print how many elements the collection holds. Zero means the selector, three means the collection was styled instead of its members.

prompt: A control declared to accept numbers holds 20. A script reads its value and compares it with the number 20 using the strict form of equality. What is the result?
optionA: True, because both are 20
optionB: False, because the value read out is text
optionC: True, but only because the control accepts numbers
optionD: An error, because the two types cannot be compared
correctAnswerText: False, because the value read out is text
explanation: A control hands back what the user typed as text whatever the control is declared to accept, so the comparison is false, because the value read out is text. The strict form refuses to convert before comparing.

prompt: A script checks a text control against undefined to see whether the user typed nothing. The user types nothing and the check still never matches. Why?
optionA: The control was not found by the lookup
optionB: The value is null rather than undefined
optionC: The check has to use the converting form of equality
optionD: An untouched control gives an empty string, which is not undefined
correctAnswerText: An untouched control gives an empty string, which is not undefined
explanation: A control always has a value and it starts as text with no characters in it, so an untouched control gives an empty string, which is not undefined. Checking the length, or comparing against an empty string, is what detects it.

prompt:
The page contains

X

. Starting from the paragraph, which element is its parent?
optionA: The section
optionB: The div
optionC: The paragraph itself
optionD: The body
correctAnswerText: The section
explanation: The section is the parent, because a parent is the element that directly contains another. The div contains that section and is therefore one level further out.

prompt: The page contains a list written across several lines, with each item on its own line. Asking the first item for its next element sibling gives the second item. Asking it for its next node instead often gives something else. What?
optionA: The list itself
optionB: The second item again, by another route
optionC: The whitespace text sitting between the two items
optionD: Nothing, in every case
correctAnswerText: The whitespace text sitting between the two items
explanation: Line breaks and indentation between tags are themselves content in the tree, so the next node is the whitespace text sitting between the two items. Asking specifically for elements is what skips it.

prompt: A lookup written with the class name but without a leading dot finds nothing, although elements carrying that class exist and the script runs late enough. What is wrong?
optionA: The script still runs too early
optionB: The selector is being read as an element name rather than a class
optionC: The class is spelled differently in the markup
optionD: A class can only be found through a collection lookup
correctAnswerText: The selector is being read as an element name rather than a class
explanation: Without the dot the text names a kind of element, and no element is called that, so the selector is being read as an element name rather than a class. Adding the dot is the whole fix.

prompt: A lookup gives null. The script sits at the bottom of the page and runs after the markup, and the same selector typed into the console afterwards also finds nothing. What is the cause?
optionA: The script ran before the element existed
optionB: The element is hidden by a stylesheet rule
optionC: The page failed to finish loading
optionD: The selector matches nothing in the page
correctAnswerText: The selector matches nothing in the page
explanation: Timing is ruled out twice over, by the script's position and by the console attempt made after loading, so the selector matches nothing in the page. A hidden element would still be found.

prompt: Two causes give the same null lookup: the script ran too early, or the selector matches nothing. Which single check separates them?
optionA: Run the same lookup in the console once the page has finished loading
optionB: Reload the page and watch whether it happens again
optionC: Move the script to the bottom of the page
optionD: Add a short wait before the lookup
correctAnswerText: Run the same lookup in the console once the page has finished loading
explanation: The two causes differ only in whether the element exists at lookup time, so run the same lookup in the console once the page has finished loading and the answer is immediate. Moving the script or adding a wait would fix one cause without ever showing which it was.

prompt: Moving a script to the bottom of the page makes a failing lookup start working. What has that established?
optionA: That the selector was wrong and has now been corrected
optionB: Nothing; the change could have fixed anything
optionC: That timing was the cause, and the selector was correct all along
optionD: That the element was hidden and is now visible
correctAnswerText: That timing was the cause, and the selector was correct all along
explanation: Only when the script runs changed, and the outcome changed with it, so timing was the cause, and the selector was correct all along. A wrong selector would still find nothing from the bottom of the page.

prompt: A lookup works on the developer's page and gives null on another page built from the same template, where that element is only rendered when there is data to show. What is the likeliest cause?
optionA: The script runs earlier on that page
optionB: On that page the element genuinely is not there
optionC: The selector is wrong and only appeared to work
optionD: That page loads the script from a different place
correctAnswerText: On that page the element genuinely is not there
explanation: The stem gives a condition under which the element is left out entirely, and the failing page is the one meeting it, so on that page the element genuinely is not there. The code is the same on both pages; the data is not.

prompt: A handler was attached by writing the function name followed by parentheses. Its message appears once while the page is loading, and clicking afterwards does nothing. What happened?
optionA: The handler was attached to the wrong element
optionB: The element did not exist when the attaching ran
optionC: Another element sits on top and swallows the clicks
optionD: The function was run at that moment and what it returned was attached instead of the function
correctAnswerText: The function was run at that moment and what it returned was attached instead of the function
explanation: The parentheses call the function there and then, which is why the message appeared during loading: the function was run at that moment and what it returned was attached instead of the function. Dropping the parentheses attaches the function itself.

prompt: Three faults all end with nothing happening on click: the handler was called instead of referenced, the element did not exist when the attaching ran, and the handler was attached to a collection. Which of them leaves a visible trace while the page loads?
optionA: The one that called the handler, because its body runs once immediately
optionB: The one attached before the element existed
optionC: The one attached to a collection
optionD: None of them leaves a trace
correctAnswerText: The one that called the handler, because its body runs once immediately
explanation: Two of the faults do nothing observable at attach time, while calling the function runs it: the one that called the handler, because its body runs once immediately, is the one that shows. That single early trace is what separates it from the other two without reading the code.

prompt: Nothing happens on click, and the console shows an error at the attaching line saying a property cannot be read of null. Which of the three faults is it?
optionA: The handler was called instead of referenced
optionB: The handler was attached to a collection
optionC: The element did not exist when the attaching ran
optionD: The body of the handler has a fault in it
correctAnswerText: The element did not exist when the attaching ran
explanation: A failed lookup gives null, and attaching to null is what raises that error at that line, so the element did not exist when the attaching ran. A fault inside the body could not report itself before any click.

prompt: Nothing happens on click, no error appears anywhere, and nothing ran while the page was loading. Which of the three faults fits?
optionA: The handler was called instead of referenced
optionB: The handler was attached to a collection rather than to its members
optionC: The element did not exist when the attaching ran
optionD: All three fit this description equally
correctAnswerText: The handler was attached to a collection rather than to its members
explanation: Calling the handler would have left a trace during loading and attaching to null would have raised an error, so the silence on both counts points at the remaining one: the handler was attached to a collection rather than to its members. Attaching to a collection succeeds and reaches nothing.

prompt: A table of fifty rows can be wired up by attaching a handler to each row, or by attaching one handler to the table and working out which row was clicked. What does the single handler cost?
optionA: Nothing; it is better in every respect
optionB: It stops working as soon as rows are added
optionC: It runs once for every row on each click
optionD: It has to work out the row itself, and gets that wrong when the markup inside a row changes
correctAnswerText: It has to work out the row itself, and gets that wrong when the markup inside a row changes
explanation: The single handler is cheaper to attach and keeps working for rows added later, and the price is that it has to work out the row itself, and gets that wrong when the markup inside a row changes. Fifty handlers know their row without asking.

prompt: A row must be shown as selected. Replacing the row's markup and adding a class to the existing row both produce the right appearance. Which has the fewest side effects?
optionA: Adding the class, because replacing the markup throws away the handlers attached to that row
optionB: Replacing the markup, because it keeps the change in one place
optionC: They are identical in effect
optionD: Replacing the markup, because a class can be overridden by the stylesheet
correctAnswerText: Adding the class, because replacing the markup throws away the handlers attached to that row
explanation: Both look right, so the choice is decided by what else changes: adding the class, because replacing the markup throws away the handlers attached to that row. New elements start with nothing attached to them.

prompt: One item in a list of two hundred has changed. Rebuilding the whole list and updating that one item both end with the right list on screen. What does rebuilding cost?
optionA: Nothing; the two are equivalent
optionB: It stops working once the list is long enough
optionC: The other items are discarded and remade, losing focus, scroll position and attached handlers
optionD: It changes the order the items appear in
correctAnswerText: The other items are discarded and remade, losing focus, scroll position and attached handlers
explanation: The screen ends up the same either way, and the difference is in what was destroyed on the way there: the other items are discarded and remade, losing focus, scroll position and attached handlers. Rebuilding is simpler to write, which is why it is chosen.

prompt: A message needs part of it in bold. Setting the paragraph's text to a string containing bold tags shows the tags as literal characters on screen. Why?
optionA: A bold element is not allowed inside a paragraph
optionB: Setting text treats everything given as characters rather than as markup
optionC: The stylesheet has removed the bolding
optionD: The text was set before the paragraph existed
correctAnswerText: Setting text treats everything given as characters rather than as markup
explanation: The two ways of putting content into an element differ exactly here: setting text treats everything given as characters rather than as markup. Setting markup instead is what would produce a bold word.

prompt: Something a user typed has to be shown back to them. Which way of putting it into the page should be preferred, and why?
optionA: Setting markup, because it is the more flexible of the two
optionB: Either; what appears on screen is the same
optionC: Setting markup, because text cannot show punctuation
optionD: Setting text, because interpreting what a user typed as markup lets it bring behaviour with it
correctAnswerText: Setting text, because interpreting what a user typed as markup lets it bring behaviour with it
explanation: The safe default is setting text, because interpreting what a user typed as markup lets it bring behaviour with it. The two only look interchangeable while the input is well behaved.

prompt: A students table holds id, name, city and marks, and contains 5 rows. What does SELECT name, city FROM students return?
optionA: All four columns, for all 5 rows
optionB: Two columns, for all 5 rows
optionC: Two columns, for the rows that have a city recorded
optionD: Two rows
correctAnswerText: Two columns, for all 5 rows
explanation: Naming columns chooses what comes back across the width of the result and leaves the rows alone, so the query returns two columns, for all 5 rows. Nothing was asked that could remove a row.

prompt: What does SELECT * FROM students return, for that same 5-row table?
optionA: Every column, for the first row only
optionB: Only the first column
optionC: Nothing until a condition is added
optionD: Every column, for all 5 rows
correctAnswerText: Every column, for all 5 rows
explanation: The star stands for the whole width of the table, so the query returns every column, for all 5 rows. A query with no condition removes nothing.

prompt: The table stores name before city. In what order do the columns arrive from SELECT city, name FROM students?
optionA: city first, then name
optionB: name first, then city, as the table stores them
optionC: In alphabetical order of the column names
optionD: In an order that cannot be relied on
correctAnswerText: city first, then name
explanation: The result is laid out in the order the query asked for, giving city first, then name. How the table stores them does not reach the caller.

prompt: How many rows does SELECT name FROM students return from that 5-row table?
optionA: One, containing all five names
optionB: Five, only if every name is different
optionC: Five
optionD: None, until a condition is added
correctAnswerText: Five
explanation: One row of the table becomes one row of the result, so five come back. Choosing a single column narrows the result rather than combining it.

prompt: Changing a query from SELECT * to SELECT name, city changes which of the following?
optionA: Both how many columns and how many rows come back
optionB: Only how many columns come back
optionC: Only how many rows come back
optionD: Neither, since the same table is read
correctAnswerText: Only how many columns come back
explanation: The choice of columns and the choice of rows are made by different parts of a query, so this changes only how many columns come back. Removing rows takes a condition.

prompt: Which query is written in a valid order?
optionA: SELECT name FROM students ORDER BY name WHERE marks > 50
optionB: SELECT name WHERE marks > 50 FROM students ORDER BY name
optionC: ORDER BY name SELECT name FROM students WHERE marks > 50
optionD: SELECT name FROM students WHERE marks > 50 ORDER BY name
correctAnswerText: SELECT name FROM students WHERE marks > 50 ORDER BY name
explanation: The parts of a query have a fixed written order: what to return, where from, which rows, then how to sort. Only SELECT name FROM students WHERE marks > 50 ORDER BY name follows it.

prompt: Students scoring above 40 are to be counted city by city. Which query is written in a valid order?
optionA: SELECT city, COUNT(*) FROM students WHERE marks > 40 GROUP BY city
optionB: SELECT city, COUNT(*) FROM students GROUP BY city WHERE marks > 40
optionC: SELECT city, COUNT(*) GROUP BY city FROM students WHERE marks > 40
optionD: GROUP BY city SELECT city, COUNT(*) FROM students WHERE marks > 40
correctAnswerText: SELECT city, COUNT(*) FROM students WHERE marks > 40 GROUP BY city
explanation: Row filtering is written before grouping, so SELECT city, COUNT(*) FROM students WHERE marks > 40 GROUP BY city is the one that will run. The others place the parts out of order.

prompt: In a written query, which comes first: naming the table, or saying how to sort?
optionA: Saying how to sort
optionB: Either; the order of the two is free
optionC: Naming the table
optionD: It depends on whether a condition is present
correctAnswerText: Naming the table
explanation: Naming the table comes first, because everything after it refers to that table. Sorting is written last of the two.

prompt: A query is written with its sorting clause before its row condition. What happens when it is run?
optionA: It runs, sorting before filtering
optionB: It does not run at all
optionC: It runs, and the sorting is ignored
optionD: It runs, and returns every row unsorted
correctAnswerText: It does not run at all
explanation: The order the parts are written in is fixed, so a query with them swapped does not run at all. This is one of the few mistakes the database refuses outright rather than answering oddly.

prompt: A scores table holds: Ana 40, Ben 55, Cara 40, Dan 70, Eve with no marks recorded. How many rows does WHERE marks > 40 return?
explanation: Only Ben and Dan are above forty, giving 2 rows. The two rows at exactly forty are not above it.

prompt: From the same scores table, how many rows does WHERE marks >= 40 return?
explanation: Ana, Ben, Cara and Dan all reach forty or more, giving 4 rows. Eve has nothing recorded and so is not among them.

prompt: From the same scores table, how many rows does WHERE name = 'Ana' return?
optionA: 0, because text cannot be compared
explanation: One row carries that name, so 1 row comes back. Text is compared just as numbers are.

prompt: From the same scores table, how many rows does WHERE marks < 60 return?
optionA: 4, counting the row with nothing recorded
explanation: Ana, Cara and Ben are below sixty, giving 3 rows. The row with nothing recorded is not below sixty, because there is no value there to compare.

prompt: A table holds: Ana/Pune/40, Ben/Pune/70, Cara/Delhi/40, Dan/Delhi/70. How many rows does WHERE city = 'Pune' AND marks > 50 return?
explanation: Only Ben is both in Pune and above fifty, so 1 row comes back. Requiring both conditions is what makes it a single row rather than three.

prompt: From the same four rows, how many does WHERE city = 'Pune' OR marks > 50 return?
explanation: Ana and Ben qualify on the city and Dan qualifies on the marks, giving 3 rows. Ben satisfies both and is still counted once.

prompt: A table holds Ana 70, Ben 50, Cara 70, Dan 60. In what sequence do the rows arrive from ORDER BY marks DESC?
optionA: Ben, then Dan, then Ana and Cara
optionB: Ana, Cara, Ben, Dan, following the stored order
optionC: Ana and Cara in some order, then Dan, then Ben
optionD: Ana, Ben, Cara, Dan, by name
correctAnswerText: Ana and Cara in some order, then Dan, then Ben
explanation: Sorting downwards puts the highest first, giving Ana and Cara in some order, then Dan, then Ben. The two seventies tie, and nothing in the query says which of them leads.

prompt: Two rows hold the same value in the column being sorted on. Which of the two comes first?
optionA: Whichever was inserted first
optionB: It is not guaranteed unless a further sorting column is given
optionC: Whichever comes first alphabetically by name
optionD: Whichever has the smaller identifier
correctAnswerText: It is not guaranteed unless a further sorting column is given
explanation: The sort has nothing left to separate the tied rows, so it is not guaranteed unless a further sorting column is given. Relying on today's order is how a report changes for no visible reason.

prompt: A table holds Ana 40, Ben 60, Cara with no marks recorded, Dan 80. What does SELECT COUNT(*) return?
explanation: Counting rows counts every row that exists, giving 4. Whether a particular column has a value in it does not come into this count.

prompt: From the same four rows, what does SELECT COUNT(marks) return?
explanation: Counting a named column counts the values present in it, and Cara has none, so the answer is 3. This is the one place the two ways of counting part company.

prompt: From the same four rows, one of which has no marks recorded, what does SELECT AVG(marks) return?
optionA: 45, because the missing row counts as a zero in the divisor
optionB: 180, which is the total rather than the average
optionC: 60, because the missing row is left out of both the total and the divisor
optionD: 80, which is the largest value present
correctAnswerText: 60, because the missing row is left out of both the total and the divisor
explanation: The total is one hundred and eighty over three values, giving 60, because the missing row is left out of both the total and the divisor. Treating the gap as a zero would give forty-five, which is what a hand calculation usually produces.

prompt: A sales table holds Pune 10, Pune 20, Delhi 30, Delhi 5, Delhi 5. How many rows does SELECT city, SUM(amount) FROM sales GROUP BY city return?
optionA: 5, one per original row
optionC: 1, holding the overall total
explanation: Grouping produces one row for each distinct value in the grouping column, and there are two cities, so 2 rows come back.

prompt: What do those returned rows hold?
optionA: Pune with 2 and Delhi with 3
optionB: A single row holding 70
optionC: Pune with 30, Delhi with 30, Delhi with 5 and Delhi with 5
optionD: Pune with 30 and Delhi with 40
correctAnswerText: Pune with 30 and Delhi with 40
explanation: Each group is collapsed to one row carrying its own total, giving Pune with 30 and Delhi with 40. Counting the rows in each group instead would give two and three.

prompt: A grouped query returns 3 rows, although the city column appears to hold only two different names when the table is read by eye. What is the likeliest cause?
optionA: Two values that look alike differ as stored text, so they group separately
optionB: Grouping always adds an extra row holding the overall total
optionC: The query grouped by the wrong column
optionD: Rows with no amount recorded form a group of their own
correctAnswerText: Two values that look alike differ as stored text, so they group separately
explanation: Grouping compares the stored values rather than their appearance, so two values that look alike differ as stored text, so they group separately. A trailing space or a difference in case is enough.

prompt: Only sales above 10 are to be included in each city's total. Which stage does that condition belong to?
optionA: The groups, after they are formed
optionB: Either stage; the result is the same
optionC: The rows, before they are grouped
optionD: The sorting, at the end
correctAnswerText: The rows, before they are grouped
explanation: The condition is about individual sales, so it belongs to the rows, before they are grouped. Applying it later would test totals rather than sales.

prompt: Two queries exist. One keeps rows whose amount is above 10 and then groups by city. The other groups by city and then keeps the groups holding more than two sales. Which answers the question "which cities made more than two sales?"
optionA: The first
optionB: The second
optionC: Both, since they end with the same cities
optionD: Neither
correctAnswerText: The second
explanation: The second is the one that answers it, because the question asks about a property of a whole city rather than of a single sale. The first can only ever discard individual sales.

prompt: A query meant to list cities with more than two sales puts the count condition among the row conditions. The database refuses to run it. Why?
optionA: The count column was not also selected
optionB: A count can only be compared using equals
optionC: The table needs an index before it can be counted
optionD: A count does not exist until rows have been grouped, so it cannot be tested row by row
correctAnswerText: A count does not exist until rows have been grouped, so it cannot be tested row by row
explanation: Row conditions are decided one row at a time, and a count belongs to a set of rows: a count does not exist until rows have been grouped, so it cannot be tested row by row. The condition has to move to the stage after grouping.

prompt: A table holds four rows: Pune/Pen, Pune/Pen, Pune/Book, Delhi/Pen. How many rows does SELECT city FROM that table return?
explanation: Every row of the table produces a row of the result whether or not its value repeats, so 4 come back. Repeats are kept unless something asks for them to be removed.

prompt: From those same four rows, how many does SELECT DISTINCT city return?
explanation: Only two different cities appear, so 2 rows come back. Removing repeats is a request, not the default.

prompt: From those same four rows, of which two are identical in both columns, how many does SELECT DISTINCT city, product return?
optionA: 2, one for each city
explanation: Repeats are judged on the whole returned row rather than on one column at a time, and only the two Pune pen rows are identical, so 3 rows come back.

prompt: A contacts table holds Ana with phone 111, Ben with no phone recorded, Cara with phone 222, Dan with no phone recorded. How many rows does WHERE phone <> '111' return?
explanation: Only Cara has a phone that is present and different, so 1 row comes back. The two rows with nothing recorded are not returned by a condition that compares against a value.

prompt: Which condition returns the rows where no phone has been recorded?
optionA: WHERE phone IS NULL
optionB: WHERE phone = NULL
optionC: WHERE phone = ''
optionD: WHERE NOT phone
correctAnswerText: WHERE phone IS NULL
explanation: A missing value cannot be compared with anything, including itself, so it takes a test of its own: WHERE phone IS NULL. Comparing with equals returns nothing at all, which looks like an empty table rather than a mistake.

prompt: The contacts table has four rows. One row matches WHERE phone = '111' and one row matches WHERE phone <> '111'. Two rows are returned by neither. Why do the two counts not add up to four?
optionA: The two conditions overlap on one row
optionB: The other two rows were removed from the table
optionC: A comparison against a missing value is neither true nor false, so those rows fall out of both
optionD: A missing value is treated as empty text, which happens to match neither
correctAnswerText: A comparison against a missing value is neither true nor false, so those rows fall out of both
explanation: Both conditions ask something about a value that is not there, and the answer is neither yes nor no: a comparison against a missing value is neither true nor false, so those rows fall out of both. Missing rows have to be asked for separately.

prompt: customers holds 3 rows: 1 Ana, 2 Ben, 3 Cara. orders holds 4 rows, belonging to customers 1, 1, 2 and 9. How many rows come back when the two are joined on the customer matching?
optionA: 7, the two row counts added
optionC: 12, every pairing
optionD: 4, one per order
explanation: Two of Ana's orders and one of Ben's find their customer, and the order belonging to customer 9 finds nobody, so 3 rows come back. Cara has no order and so contributes nothing.

prompt: The same two tables are combined with the matching condition left out, and the result has 12 rows. What has happened?
optionA: Each table was read twice over
optionB: The database duplicated rows to make the two tables the same size
optionC: The two tables were read in full and placed one after the other
optionD: Every customer has been paired with every order, because nothing said which rows correspond
correctAnswerText: Every customer has been paired with every order, because nothing said which rows correspond
explanation: Three customers and four orders give twelve pairings, which is exactly what appears: every customer has been paired with every order, because nothing said which rows correspond. Placing the tables one after the other would have given seven rows.

prompt: Which query answers exactly the question "which students scored at least 50?"
optionA: SELECT name FROM students WHERE marks >= 50
optionB: SELECT name FROM students WHERE marks > 50
optionC: SELECT * FROM students WHERE marks >= 50
optionD: SELECT name FROM students WHERE marks <= 50
correctAnswerText: SELECT name FROM students WHERE marks >= 50
explanation: At least fifty includes fifty itself and asks for the students rather than everything known about them, so SELECT name FROM students WHERE marks >= 50 is the exact answer. Two of the others run perfectly well and answer a slightly different question.

prompt: Which query answers exactly the question "which cities have more than one student?"
optionA: SELECT city FROM students WHERE COUNT(*) > 1
optionB: SELECT city, COUNT(*) FROM students GROUP BY city
optionC: SELECT city FROM students GROUP BY city HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
optionD: SELECT DISTINCT city FROM students
correctAnswerText: SELECT city FROM students GROUP BY city HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
explanation: The question tests a property of each city and asks only for the cities, so SELECT city FROM students GROUP BY city HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 answers it. One of the others will not run, and two run but answer a neighbouring question instead.

prompt: A report joins customers to orders and to addresses, then totals each customer's orders. Each customer appears once, and every total is several times too large. What is the fault?
optionA: The amounts are stored in the wrong unit
optionB: Each order is counted once per address, because the second join multiplies the rows
optionC: The row condition was applied after the grouping
optionD: Some orders have no amount recorded
correctAnswerText: Each order is counted once per address, because the second join multiplies the rows
explanation: Grouping hides the multiplication, because the extra rows are folded back into one row per customer before anybody sees them: each order is counted once per address, because the second join multiplies the rows. A customer with three addresses reports three times the truth.

prompt: An average reported by a query is higher than the same average worked out by hand, in which blank entries were treated as zeroes. Nothing else differs between the two. What accounts for the gap?
optionA: The query rounds its result upwards
optionB: A row condition removed the lowest values
optionC: The average was taken over a different column
optionD: The query leaves the blank entries out of both the total and the divisor
correctAnswerText: The query leaves the blank entries out of both the total and the divisor
explanation: Both calculations use the same rows and the same column, and they differ only in what a blank entry contributes: the query leaves the blank entries out of both the total and the divisor. The hand calculation divides by a larger number and so reports less.

prompt: Three faults can each make a reported total wrong: a join with nothing to match on, a condition applied at the wrong stage, and values that are not recorded. Which single check shows whether row multiplication is to blame?
optionA: Count the rows the query produces before grouping and compare that with the number of source rows
optionB: Look at the average instead of the total
optionC: Add a request to remove duplicate rows and see whether the total changes
optionD: Run the query a second time
correctAnswerText: Count the rows the query produces before grouping and compare that with the number of source rows
explanation: Multiplication is visible only before the grouping folds it away, so count the rows the query produces before grouping and compare that with the number of source rows. Removing duplicates would change the total without ever showing why.

prompt: Adding a request to remove duplicate rows makes an inflated total come out right. What has that established?
optionA: That the join was correct all along
optionB: That the amounts themselves were wrong
optionC: That rows were being multiplied; the join is still wrong and the symptom is now hidden
optionD: Nothing at all about the cause
correctAnswerText: That rows were being multiplied; the join is still wrong and the symptom is now hidden
explanation: The fix would do nothing unless duplicate rows existed, so rows were being multiplied; the join is still wrong and the symptom is now hidden. The next total that involves a genuinely repeated amount will be wrong in the other direction.

prompt: A report is correct on the small sample a developer tested and wrong on the full data, where some customers have more than one address on file. What is the likeliest cause?
optionA: The full data is too large for the query to handle
optionB: The join multiplies rows only for customers who have more than one matching address
optionC: The sample was filtered differently from the full data
optionD: The totals grow too large to be stored
correctAnswerText: The join multiplies rows only for customers who have more than one matching address
explanation: The fault needs a customer with several matching rows before it can appear at all, which the sample happened not to contain: the join multiplies rows only for customers who have more than one matching address. Sample data that is too tidy hides this class of fault entirely.

prompt: No rows in the table satisfy the condition. The query asks for a count of the matching rows. What comes back?
optionA: No rows at all
optionB: An error
optionC: One row, holding nothing
optionD: One row, holding 0
correctAnswerText: One row, holding 0
explanation: A count over nothing is a perfectly good answer, so one row, holding 0 comes back. An empty result is not a failure and nothing is raised.

prompt: Again no rows satisfy the condition, and this time the query asks for the average of a column. What comes back?
optionA: One row, holding no value
optionB: One row, holding 0
optionC: No rows at all
optionD: An error
correctAnswerText: One row, holding no value
explanation: There is nothing to divide and nothing to divide by, so one row, holding no value comes back. A program that adds this to a running total without checking will produce nothing rather than the total it had.

prompt: Why do a count and an average behave differently when nothing matches?
optionA: A count is calculated more cheaply than an average
optionB: An average also returns zero, and the difference is only in how it is displayed
optionC: Counting nothing has an answer, which is zero, and averaging nothing has none
optionD: A count also returns nothing, and the difference is only in how it is displayed
correctAnswerText: Counting nothing has an answer, which is zero, and averaging nothing has none
explanation: The two summaries differ in whether the empty case has a sensible value at all: counting nothing has an answer, which is zero, and averaging nothing has none. Inventing a zero average would claim a measurement that was never made.

prompt: A grouped query is run over a table in which no rows satisfy the condition. How many rows come back?
optionA: One, holding a zero for the whole table
optionB: None, because groups are formed only out of rows that matched
optionC: One for each group that would have existed
optionD: An error, because there is nothing to group
correctAnswerText: None, because groups are formed only out of rows that matched
explanation: Grouping has nothing to work with once the condition has removed everything, so none come back, because groups are formed only out of rows that matched. This differs from an ungrouped count, which still answers with a single zero.

prompt: An empty result can be handled by having the query substitute a zero, or by letting the program that reads the result treat no rows as zero. What does the substitution cost?
optionA: Nothing; it is simply more convenient
optionB: The query stops working on large tables
optionC: The result comes back with a different number of columns
optionD: The result can no longer distinguish nothing measured from a measurement of zero
correctAnswerText: The result can no longer distinguish nothing measured from a measurement of zero
explanation: Substituting inside the query is convenient and loses information at the same moment: the result can no longer distinguish nothing measured from a measurement of zero. A report of zero sales and a report of no data are different claims.

prompt: One query keeps rows above 50 and then groups them. Another groups first and keeps the groups whose largest value is above 50. They agree on the sample data, in which every group holds either all values above 50 or none. Are they equivalent?
optionA: No; they part company as soon as one group holds values on both sides of 50
optionB: Yes; both end with the same groups
optionC: No; the second one will not run
optionD: Yes, as long as the data stays sorted
correctAnswerText: No; they part company as soon as one group holds values on both sides of 50
explanation: The sample cannot separate them because no group mixes the two kinds of row: they part company as soon as one group holds values on both sides of 50. The first then drops the low rows from its totals and the second keeps them.

prompt: Two conditions are written: WHERE phone <> '111' and WHERE NOT (phone = '111'). What data separates them?
optionA: Rows with no phone recorded, which only the second returns
optionB: Rows whose phone is exactly 111
optionC: None; both leave out the rows where no phone is recorded
optionD: Rows whose phone is empty text
correctAnswerText: None; both leave out the rows where no phone is recorded
explanation: Both forms ask a question about a value that is not there and get no answer either way, so none; both leave out the rows where no phone is recorded. Negating a comparison does not turn an unanswerable comparison into a true one.

prompt: Two queries count each customer's orders. One joins the two tables and counts the joined rows. The other keeps every customer and counts the orders that match. They agree on data in which every customer has at least one order. Are they equivalent?
optionA: Yes; both count exactly the same orders
optionB: No; they differ for a customer with no orders, whom only the second reports
optionC: No; the first will not run when a customer has no orders
optionD: Yes, provided the two tables hold the same number of rows
correctAnswerText: No; they differ for a customer with no orders, whom only the second reports
explanation: A customer with no orders contributes no joined row at all, so they differ for a customer with no orders, whom only the second reports. The sample could not show it because no such customer was in it.

prompt: A query is rewritten to run faster and returns the same rows as the original on today's data. What would justify calling the rewrite safe?
optionA: Showing that the rewrite is measurably faster
optionB: Showing that both return the same number of rows
optionC: Showing that both read the same tables
optionD: Showing the two agree on data containing unrecorded values and unmatched rows as well
correctAnswerText: Showing the two agree on data containing unrecorded values and unmatched rows as well
explanation: Today's data is one sample and the rewrite has to hold for the data the table will contain, so the case rests on showing the two agree on data containing unrecorded values and unmatched rows as well. Those are the two places query rewrites usually part company.

prompt: Someone spends their day writing and reviewing the code that runs a company's website. Which role is that?
optionA: Data analyst
optionB: Software developer
optionC: Project manager
optionD: Systems administrator
correctAnswerText: Software developer
explanation: Writing and reviewing code is the developer's daily work. An analyst works with data, a manager coordinates the work, and an administrator keeps the systems running.

prompt: Someone spends their day writing queries against a database and preparing reports on what the numbers show. Which role is that?
optionA: Software developer
optionB: Database administrator
optionC: Support engineer
optionD: Data analyst
correctAnswerText: Data analyst
explanation: Querying data and reporting on it is analysis. A database administrator keeps the database itself running, which is adjacent work with different accountability.

prompt: Someone spends their day investigating problems reported by customers and telling the engineering team what is reproducible. Which role is that?
optionA: Support engineer
optionB: Software developer
optionC: Project manager
optionD: Data analyst
correctAnswerText: Support engineer
explanation: Reproducing reported problems and passing them on is support work. A developer may fix what is found, which is the next step rather than the same job.

prompt: Someone spends their day setting up the machines an application runs on and keeping them available. Which role is that?
optionA: Software developer
optionB: Data analyst
optionC: Systems administrator
optionD: Support engineer
correctAnswerText: Systems administrator
explanation: Preparing and maintaining the machines is administration. Writing what runs on them is a different job, though in a small team one person may do both.

prompt: In a very small company, one person writes the code, sets up the servers and answers customer problems. What does that show about roles?
optionA: That the roles are not really distinct
optionB: The work is the same in any company; who does it depends on how many people there are
optionC: That small companies do not need specialists
optionD: That the person holds three jobs at once
correctAnswerText: The work is the same in any company; who does it depends on how many people there are
explanation: The tasks do not merge when one person does them all, which is why a larger team can split them along the same lines. What varies is the division of labour rather than the work.

prompt: What job does a CV do?
optionA: Proves what someone has done
optionB: Lists every task someone has ever performed
optionC: Replaces the need for an interview
optionD: States what someone claims to have done, so a reader can decide whether to look further
correctAnswerText: States what someone claims to have done, so a reader can decide whether to look further
explanation: A CV is a set of claims, which is why it opens a conversation rather than settling one. Anything that could be checked independently is evidence, and a CV is where it is pointed at.

prompt: What job does a portfolio of projects do?
optionA: Shows work a reader can examine for themselves
optionB: Lists the technologies someone has used
optionC: Proves someone worked hard
optionD: Replaces a CV entirely
correctAnswerText: Shows work a reader can examine for themselves
explanation: A portfolio is checkable in a way a claim is not, which is the whole reason for having one. A list of technologies is another claim, in a different format.

prompt: What job does a reference do?
optionA: Adds a formality to the application
optionB: Proves the candidate is a good person
optionC: Lets somebody who worked with the candidate confirm what they did
optionD: Replaces the need for evidence of work
correctAnswerText: Lets somebody who worked with the candidate confirm what they did
explanation: A reference converts a claim into something another person will stand behind. Treating it as a formality is what makes candidates choose referees who cannot say anything specific.

prompt: A candidate needs to show they can build a working application. Which artefact serves that best?
optionA: A CV line saying they can build applications
optionB: A project the reader can run or read
optionC: A certificate from a course about building applications
optionD: A reference saying they are hard-working
correctAnswerText: A project the reader can run or read
explanation: Only one of these lets the reader check the claim rather than accept it. A certificate shows a course was completed, which is a different fact.

prompt: What does an internship expect a candidate to show?
optionA: Several years of experience in the role
optionB: Nothing at all
optionC: A completed degree in the subject
optionD: Enough foundation to learn quickly, rather than experience of the work
correctAnswerText: Enough foundation to learn quickly, rather than experience of the work
explanation: An internship exists to provide the experience, so demanding it would defeat the purpose. That does not make it open to anyone regardless of preparation.

prompt: What does a graduate role expect a candidate to show?
optionA: Foundations and evidence of learning, with training expected on the job
optionB: Nothing, since training is provided
optionC: The same experience as an established developer
optionD: Only a qualification, with nothing further
correctAnswerText: Foundations and evidence of learning, with training expected on the job
explanation: Training being provided sets the level rather than removing the requirement. A qualification is part of what is looked at and rarely the whole of it.

prompt: Is a qualification on its own usually enough to obtain a first role?
optionA: Yes; a qualification is what employers ask for
optionB: No; qualifications are not considered at all
optionC: Rarely; it is one signal among several and says little about what someone can build
optionD: Yes, provided the grade is high enough
correctAnswerText: Rarely; it is one signal among several and says little about what someone can build
explanation: A qualification establishes that a course was completed and leaves open what the candidate can do unsupervised. It is genuinely considered, which is why the answer is "rarely enough" rather than "irrelevant".

prompt: Two routes into a first role are an internship and a graduate programme. What most distinguishes what they expect?
optionA: The internship expects more experience
optionB: The internship expects less prior evidence and offers less certainty of a continuing role
optionC: The graduate programme expects no preparation
optionD: They expect exactly the same things
correctAnswerText: The internship expects less prior evidence and offers less certainty of a continuing role
explanation: The two differ in what they ask for and in what they promise, and both differences run in the same direction. Neither expects nothing.

prompt: Which skill does a data analyst's work depend on most?
optionA: Knowing one particular spreadsheet product
optionB: Communicating clearly, which every role needs
optionC: Designing user interfaces
optionD: Reasoning about what data does and does not support
correctAnswerText: Reasoning about what data does and does not support
explanation: The underlying skill is judgement about evidence; the tools change and the judgement does not. Communication matters everywhere and so does not distinguish this role from any other.

prompt: A job advertisement lists a particular framework. What is the underlying skill it is standing in for?
optionA: Building applications of that kind, which the framework is one way of doing
optionB: Familiarity with that framework and nothing else
optionC: Willingness to learn new tools
optionD: Experience of working in a team
correctAnswerText: Building applications of that kind, which the framework is one way of doing
explanation: A named tool is usually shorthand for the work it is used for, which is why someone with the skill in a different tool is often considered. Reading it as the requirement itself narrows the field to people who happen to have used one product.

prompt: Which of these statements about a candidate can somebody else check?
optionA: That they are passionate about technology
optionB: That they worked very hard on their studies
optionC: A public repository containing an application they wrote
optionD: That they are a fast learner
correctAnswerText: A public repository containing an application they wrote
explanation: Only one of these points at something a reader can open and examine. The others are self-assessments, which may be entirely true and cannot be confirmed by anyone else.

prompt: A candidate lists "completed an online course in databases". Is that evidence of the skill?
optionA: Yes; the course covered the skill
optionB: It is evidence the course was completed, and shows nothing that was built with it
optionC: No; courses are worthless
optionD: Yes, provided the course was long enough
